# Methods

<!-- Generated by tools/build_methods_md.mjs from src/methods/content.js. Do not edit: change the source and rebuild. -->

What Exoplanet Science Lab computes and how: the equations as implemented, the parameters and their default priors, the numerical method with its measured accuracy, the assumptions and known limits, and the references. Written to be cited and adapted in the methods section of a paper.

This is the Markdown copy of the site's Methods page (`methods/`, https://exoplanet.science/methods/). Equations are written in LaTeX between dollar signs.

Each section below describes one technique as the source code implements it; the file is named under the heading. Accuracy statements link to the test or the [Validation](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-summary) entry that produces the number. Where something is not modelled, was not tested, or disagrees with a published value, the section says so under "Assumptions and limits".

Notation: $R_\star$, $M_\star$ stellar radius and mass; $k = R_p/R_\star$; $a/R_\star$ scaled semi-major axis; $i$ inclination; $P$ period; $T_0$ mid-transit time; $e$, $\omega$ eccentricity and argument of periastron; $\nu$, $E$, $M$ true, eccentric and mean anomaly; $\mu = \sqrt{1 - r^2}$ with $r$ the projected distance from the centre of the stellar disc in stellar radii.

## 1. Time standards and conventions

Code: `src/core/kepler.js`, `src/core/data.js`, `src/core/fits.js`, `src/core/observability.js`, `src/core/derive.js`

### Geometry

The sky plane is $X, Y$ in units of the stellar radius and $+Z$ points to the observer. With $u = \omega + \nu$ the planet is at

$$
X = -r\cos u, \qquad Y = -r \sin u \cos i, \qquad Z = r \sin u \sin i, \qquad r = \frac{a}{R_\star}\,(1 - e\cos E)
$$

so the planet is in front of the star when $Z > 0$. Mid-transit $T_0$ is inferior conjunction, $\omega + \nu = \pi/2$; mid-eclipse is superior conjunction, $\omega + \nu = -\pi/2$. These are not the times of smallest projected separation on an inclined eccentric orbit (see [Kepler solver and orbits](#orbits)). Radial velocities are positive when the star recedes. $\omega$ is the same number as the $\omega$ of radvel and pyaneti ([Validation: sign and angle conventions](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#rv-conventions)).

### Times in the analyzer

Times are used as given. The reader (`parseLightCurve`) recognises the zero point of the time column from a header or from the size of the numbers (JD; MJD = JD − 2400000.5; RJD = JD − 2400000; BTJD = JD − 2457000; BKJD = JD − 2454833) and adds it; it does **not** convert between time scales (UTC, TT, TDB) or between geocentric, heliocentric and barycentric times. Inside a fit, times are measured from an integer reference (`data.tRef`, the floor of the first time) so that Julian dates keep their precision in double arithmetic; results are reported as absolute times again. Catalogue epochs are taken as the catalogue lists them and assumed to be $\mathrm{BJD}_\mathrm{TDB}$; a different stated time system is flagged, not converted.

### Times from image headers

The photometry page converts the UTC mid-exposure time of each frame to $\mathrm{BJD}_\mathrm{TDB}$ [Eastman et al. 2010](#ref-eastman2010) when the target coordinates are known (`utcToBjdTdb`):

$$
\mathrm{BJD}_\mathrm{TDB} = \mathrm{JD}_\mathrm{UTC} + \frac{\Delta\mathrm{AT} + 32.184\,\mathrm{s} + 0.001657\,\mathrm{s}\,\sin g + 0.000014\,\mathrm{s}\,\sin 2g}{86400\,\mathrm{s}} + \frac{\mathbf{r}_\oplus \cdot \hat{n}}{c}
$$

with $\Delta\mathrm{AT}$ = TAI − UTC from a leap-second table (1972 to 2017-01-01, 37 s held afterwards), $g = 357.53^\circ + 0.9856003^\circ\,(\mathrm{JD} - 2451545.0)$, $\hat{n}$ the unit vector of the target's ICRS coordinates, and $\mathbf{r}_\oplus$ the Earth's barycentric position: the low-precision solar theory of [Meeus 1998](#ref-meeus1998) (chapter 25) for the heliocentric Earth plus the Sun's offset from the barycentre due to Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune from the Keplerian elements of [Standish & Williams (JPL)](#ref-standish). The mid-exposure time is the header's start time plus half the exposure, unless the keyword or its comment says it is already a mid or end time; TAI, GPS, TT and TDB header times are first converted to UTC.

The planner uses a second, simpler conversion (`jdUtcToBjdTdb` in `observability.js`): the light time to the Sun's centre instead of the barycentre, and TDB = TT.

### Constants

`src/core/derive.js`: $R_\odot$ = 6.957e8 m, $R_\mathrm{Jup}$ = 7.1492e7 m, $R_\oplus$ = 6.3781e6 m, au = 1.495978707e11 m, $GM_\odot$ = 1.32712440018e20 m³ s⁻², $M_\mathrm{Jup}/M_\odot$ = 9.5459426398e-4, $G$ = 6.6743e-11 (SI), $T_{\mathrm{eff},\odot}$ = 5772 K, day = 86400 s.

### Accuracy and checks

- UTC to BJD_TDB, 35 targets and dates: within 0.045 s. ([Validation: From images to a light curve](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-photometry); `test/fits.test.mjs`)
- Barycentric time correction (BJD_TDB − JD_UTC): worst 3.92 s. ([Validation: Which transits can be observed](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-planner); `test/observability.test.mjs`)
- Sign and $\omega$ convention against radvel, pyaneti and a reference obtained by differentiating the orbit in 30-digit arithmetic: `node test/validation.test.mjs` ("sign", "omega").

### Assumptions and limits

- No conversion between time standards in the analyzer, the Timing tab, the catalogue or the planner's input: mixing $\mathrm{BJD}_\mathrm{TDB}$ with $\mathrm{JD}_\mathrm{UTC}$ or HJD moves a mid-transit time by up to about 8 minutes (heliocentric correction) plus 69 s (TDB − UTC in 2017 and later). The user must supply one consistent time standard.
- The header conversion leaves out the observatory's position on the Earth (up to 21 ms), the Shapiro delay, parallax and proper motion. HJD header times are passed through unconverted. The leap-second table ends in 2017.
- The project has three separate implementations of Sun position and time conversion (`fits.js`, `astro.js`, `observability.js`) with different accuracy; they have not been merged.

References: [Eastman et al. 2010](#ref-eastman2010); [Meeus 1998](#ref-meeus1998); [Standish & Williams (JPL)](#ref-standish); [Astropy Collaboration 2022](#ref-astropy2022).

## 2. Transit model and limb darkening

Code: `src/core/transit.js`, `src/core/limbdark.js`, `src/core/ldest.js`, `src/core/ldspec.js`, `tools/build_ld_table.py`, `tools/build_ld_spectral.py`

### Limb-darkening laws

Every law is mapped onto the four-coefficient law of [Claret 2000](#ref-claret2000),

$$
\frac{I(\mu)}{I(1)} = 1 - \sum_{n=1}^{4} a_n \left(1 - \mu^{n/2}\right), \qquad \mu = \sqrt{1 - r^2}
$$

of which the others are exact special cases: linear $I = 1 - u(1-\mu)$ is $a_2 = u$; quadratic $I = 1 - u_1(1-\mu) - u_2(1-\mu)^2$ is $a_2 = u_1 + 2u_2$, $a_4 = -u_2$; the $(q_1, q_2)$ form of [Kipping 2013](#ref-kipping2013) is the quadratic law with $u_1 = 2\sqrt{q_1}\,q_2$, $u_2 = \sqrt{q_1}\,(1 - 2q_2)$; the square-root law $I = 1 - c(1-\mu) - d(1-\sqrt{\mu})$ is $a_1 = d$, $a_2 = c$. A profile that is negative anywhere, brightens toward the limb, or has non-positive total flux is outside the prior: the likelihood rejects it (tested on 25 values of $\mu$).

### Flux

With $F(r) = \int_0^r I(r')\,r'\,dr'$, which is in closed form for this law, the vector field $F(r)/r^2\,(x, y)$ has divergence $I(r)$, so the flux behind the planet's disc is a line integral around the boundary of the occulted region (Green's theorem):

$$
\frac{\Delta F}{F} = \frac{1}{2\pi F(1)} \oint \frac{F(r)}{r^2}\,(x\,dy - y\,dx), \qquad F(1) = \frac{1 - \sum a_n}{2} + \frac{a_1}{2.5} + \frac{a_2}{3} + \frac{a_3}{3.5} + \frac{a_4}{4}
$$

The boundary is an arc of the planet's limb, parametrised by the angle $\varphi$ about the planet's centre, plus, during ingress and egress, an arc of the stellar limb where the integrand is the constant $F(1)$ and the contribution is analytic. With the planet's centre at projected distance $z$ and radius $p$, $r^2 = z^2 + p^2 + 2zp\cos\varphi$ along the planet's limb. When the planet is wholly on the disc, further than 0.02 stellar radii from the limb and not covering the centre, the integrand is smooth and periodic and a 12-node midpoint rule is used. Otherwise the arc is integrated with 20 Gauss-Legendre nodes after the substitution $\varphi = \varphi_A + (\pi - \varphi_A)u^2$, which removes the square-root branch point where the arc meets the stellar limb. Near the stellar centre ($r^2 < 10^{-3}$) $F(r)/r^2$ is evaluated by a series. A uniform disc uses the closed-form overlap area of two circles. The model flux is $1 - \Delta F/F$ when the planet is in front ($Z > 0$) and 1 otherwise.

### Where the coefficients come from

- **Free parameters**, sampled with the other parameters.
- **A model-atmosphere table** (`src/data/ld_table.js`, built by `tools/build_ld_table.py`): PHOENIX-ACES specific intensities [Husser et al. 2013](#ref-husser2013), obtained through the file list and cache of LDTK [Parviainen & Aigrain 2015](#ref-parviainen2015ldtk), integrated with photon weighting over 37 passbands for $T_\mathrm{eff}$ = 2300 to 8000 K, $\log g$ = 4.0, 4.5, 5.0 (5.5 at or below 4000 K) and [Fe/H] = −0.5, 0, +0.5. Measured response curves (those shipped with pylightcurve) are used for TESS, Kepler, CHEOPS, Johnson UBV, Cousins RI, SDSS ugriz and 2MASS JHKs; the remaining bands are boxcars. The stellar limb is placed at the steepest gradient of the model intensity and the radius rescaled to it, as in ExoTETHyS [Morello et al. 2020](#ref-morello2020); the four-coefficient law is fitted by least squares for $\mu \ge 0.1$, and refitted under constraints when the unconstrained fit is not monotonic or goes negative. The other laws are fitted to that profile (constrained to physical coefficients). The application interpolates trilinearly in $T_\mathrm{eff}$, $\log g$ and [Fe/H] and clamps, with a flag, outside the grid.
- **Any wavelength range** (`src/core/ldspec.js`, table built by `tools/build_ld_spectral.py`): the same models in 357 bins from 200 to 5500 nm, stored as a mean plus 40 principal components. The profile of a band is the flux- and response-weighted mean of the bins' profiles, $I_\mathrm{band}(\mu) = \sum_b w_b F_b I_b(\mu) / \sum_b w_b F_b$, then constrained to be physical.
- **A grey atmosphere** (fallback when no table applies): $I(\mu) \propto \int_0^\infty B_\lambda[T(\mu x)]\,e^{-x}\,dx$ with $T^4 = \frac{3}{4}T_\mathrm{eff}^4\,[\tau + q(\tau)]$, $q(\tau) = 0.7104 - 0.1331\,e^{-3.4488\tau}$, averaged over nine wavelengths of the band with photon weighting; the law is then fitted by least squares on 60 values of $\mu$ from 0.02 to 1. It depends on $T_\mathrm{eff}$ and wavelength only.
- **Following the star** in a fit: $T_\mathrm{eff}$ (and [Fe/H] when a table is in use) are sampled with priors at their measured uncertainties, and the coefficients are computed from each sample (`makeLDTie`: tabulated once per fit on 17 × 7 knots plus every table node inside the prior, bilinear in between). The coefficients are then confined to the family a star of that kind can produce.

### Accuracy and checks

- Flux against scipy adaptive quadrature of the area integral on an orbit computed in 30-digit arithmetic, 41 light curves (uniform, linear, quadratic and four-coefficient laws; $k$ from 0.01 to 0.3; grazing; $e$ up to 0.93): worst error 3.1e-11, tolerance 1e-10; at the kernel's branch points (contacts, centre) 1.4e-10. Printed by `node test/validation.test.mjs`, recomputed in the [Validation tab](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-transit).
- Kernel alone against scipy quadrature over 680 geometries ($k$ from 0.01 to 1.2) and five profiles: `node test/kernel.test.mjs`.
- HD 80606, TESS band, against the coefficients EXOTIC’s examples use: 0.56 ppm in flux. ([Validation: Limb darkening from stellar parameters](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-limbdark); `test/limbdark.test.mjs`)
- Four-coefficient law, worst spectral type (K): I(μ) rms 0.0009; 12.9 ppm in a transit. ([Validation: Limb darkening from stellar parameters](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-limbdark); `test/limbdark.test.mjs`)
- Quadratic law, worst spectral type (M): I(μ) rms 0.0029; 20.8 ppm. ([Validation: Limb darkening from stellar parameters](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-limbdark); `test/limbdark.test.mjs`)
- Same table against ATLAS models (different atmosphere physics): worst I(μ) rms 0.0327: the model-to-model spread dominates. ([Validation: Limb darkening from stellar parameters](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-limbdark); `test/limbdark.test.mjs`)
- Any wavelength range (357 bins, 200 to 5500 nm): 39 HST/WFC3 channels: I(μ) rms median 4.8e-4, worst 9.2e-3; transit depth within 0.72%. ([Validation: Limb darkening from stellar parameters](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-limbdark); `test/ldspec.test.mjs`)
- Transit model against pylightcurve, five planets up to e = 0.93: largest flux difference 1.0e-7. ([Validation: EXOTIC’s own examples, reproduced](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-exotic); `test/exotic.test.mjs`)
- Flux dips exactly when the discs overlap: 160,000 samples, 0 mismatches. ([Validation: Evidence, ephemerides and geometry](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-basics); `test/physics.test.mjs`)

### Assumptions and limits

- The flux is accurate to about 1e-10, not to rounding error; the closed form of [Agol, Luger & Foreman-Mackey 2020](#ref-agol2020) for the quadratic law is more accurate and faster. Every law is integrated numerically here.
- Not modelled: star spots and faculae, stellar oblateness and gravity darkening, planetary oblateness, rings, refraction, the planet's night-side emission during transit (unless the phase-curve model is on). Dilution by other stars in the aperture is an optional term of the likelihood ([The likelihood](#likelihood)); the bundled TESS light curve of HD 80606 is diluted by HD 80607, and its stored example result is fitted without that term.
- One limb-darkening law and band for all light curves in a fit (no multi-band fits).
- The comparison with ExoTETHyS tests the processing, the grid and the interpolation, not the atmosphere physics: both start from the same PHOENIX files. PHOENIX and ATLAS models differ by 0.0125 rms in $I(\mu)$ on average, which is larger than every processing error quoted here. The boxcar and JWST bands have no external reference. Below $\mu = 0.1$ the profile is an extrapolation. Stars outside the grid are clamped to its edge. Beyond 5.5 µm there is no table.

References: [Claret 2000](#ref-claret2000); [Kipping 2013](#ref-kipping2013); [Husser et al. 2013](#ref-husser2013); [Parviainen & Aigrain 2015](#ref-parviainen2015ldtk); [Morello et al. 2020](#ref-morello2020); [Agol, Luger & Foreman-Mackey 2020](#ref-agol2020); [Tsiaras et al. 2016](#ref-tsiaras2016).

## 3. Exposure averaging

Code: `src/core/model.js (autoSupersample)`, `src/core/transit.js (transitModel)`, `src/core/session.js`

A detector integrates the flux over each exposure. When an exposure time $\Delta t$ is given, the model at time $t_i$ is the mean of $n$ evaluations at the centres of $n$ equal slices of the exposure:

$$
\bar{f}(t_i) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} f\!\left(t_i + \left(j - \frac{n-1}{2}\right)\frac{\Delta t}{n}\right)
$$

With several planets the product of the planets' fluxes is averaged, not the product of the averages. The number of sub-samples is chosen automatically from the ingress duration $\tau = (T_{14} - T_{23})/2$ (closed-form durations, at least 1e-4 d) and the depth $\delta = k^2$:

$$
n = \left\lceil \frac{\Delta t}{\tau} \sqrt{\frac{\delta}{6 \times 10^{-6}}} \right\rceil, \quad \text{made odd, at most 41; } n = 1 \text{ when the expression is } \le 1
$$

This follows from the error of the midpoint rule, about (curvature) × $(\Delta t/n)^2/24$ with a curvature of order $4\delta/\tau^2$ during ingress, for a target of 1 ppm. Each epoch of a light curve may carry its own exposure time and then gets its own $n$.

### Accuracy and checks

- Against the mean of 4001 evaluations of the exact quadratic-law flux (`node test/validation.test.mjs`): 30 min exposures of a hot Jupiter (ingress 21 min), automatic $n$ = 41: 5.0e-7; 2 min exposures of the same planet, $n$ = 5: 6.9e-7; 30 min exposures of a small planet on a 1 d orbit (ingress 1.6 min), $n$ = 41: 1.3e-7; with 101 sub-samples the three cases give 7.4e-8, 1.7e-9 and 1.3e-8. See [Validation: exposure averaging](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#transit-exposure).

### Assumptions and limits

- The count is capped at 41, so the residual grows for exposures much longer than ingress; the analyzer offers no manual setting; a count can be given by hand only through the programming interface (`spec.supersample` and `segments[s].supersample` of `buildProblem`).
- The exposure is assumed to be a uniform window centred on the time stamp, with no dead time and no read-out weighting. The exposure time is whatever the user or the file header supplies.
- The count is chosen once, from the parameter values at the start of a fit, not re-evaluated for each sample. Because a session saved after a fit holds the fitted values, re-running a stored session can choose a different count: `hd80606-tess.json` re-runs to 12,813 likelihood calls instead of the stored 12,837 (0.004σ in the result).

References: [Winn 2010](#ref-winn2010).

<a id="orbits"></a>

## 4. Kepler solver and orbits

Code: `src/core/kepler.js`

The mean anomaly is $M(t) = M_0 + 2\pi (t - T_0)/P$, with $M_0$ the mean anomaly at inferior conjunction: $\nu_c = \pi/2 - \omega$, $E_c = 2\arctan\!\left[\sqrt{(1-e)/(1+e)}\,\tan(\nu_c/2)\right]$, $M_0 = E_c - e\sin E_c$. Kepler's equation $E - e\sin E = M$ is solved from the starting value $E_0 = M + 0.85\,e\,\mathrm{sgn}(\sin M)$ [Danby 1987](#ref-danby1987) with the update

$$
\delta_1 = -\frac{f}{f'}, \quad \delta_2 = -\frac{f}{f' + \frac{1}{2}\delta_1 f''}, \quad \delta_3 = -\frac{f}{f' + \frac{1}{2}\delta_2 f'' + \frac{1}{6}\delta_2^2 f'''}, \quad E \leftarrow E + \delta_3
$$

where $f = E - e\sin E - M$, iterated until $|\delta_3| < 10^{-15}\max(1, |E|)$ (at most 30 iterations; two to four are needed). The true anomaly is $\nu = 2\,\mathrm{atan2}\!\left(\sqrt{1+e}\,\sin\frac{E}{2},\ \sqrt{1-e}\,\cos\frac{E}{2}\right)$. Eccentricities are limited to $e \le 0.999$. Circular orbits skip the solver.

Event times follow from the anomaly of the event: periastron $\nu = 0$, mid-eclipse $\omega + \nu = -\pi/2$. Durations ($T_{14}$, $T_{23}$ and the eclipse equivalents $E_{14}$, $E_{23}$) are found numerically: the time at which the projected separation equals $1 \pm k$ is bracketed from the conjunction and refined by 60 bisections, on each side. The closed-form durations of [Winn 2010](#ref-winn2010) (eqs. 14 to 16) are used only to choose the exposure sub-sampling and for catalogue estimates. The impact parameter is $b = (a/R_\star)\cos i\,(1 - e^2)/(1 + e\sin\omega)$.

### Accuracy and checks

- `node test/validation.test.mjs`, against 30-digit arithmetic: true anomaly within 2.4e-15 rad for $e$ = 0.05 to 0.999 (residual of the equation 4.4e-16); periastron and eclipse times of 21 orbits within 2.3e-10 s; $T_{14}$, $T_{23}$, $E_{14}$, $E_{23}$ of 10 orbits within 1.3e-10 s. The closed-form duration is exact for circular orbits and up to 0.91% short otherwise. See [Validation: the orbit and its timing](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-orbit).

### Assumptions and limits

- **One published number is not reproduced.** For HD 80606 b this code gives an eclipse duration $E_{14}$ = 0.08337 d, equal to root finding on the 30-digit orbit (0.08337 d); [Pearson et al. 2022](#ref-pearson2022) list 0.0717 d. The transit duration agrees (0.4985 d against 0.499 d). No method tried reproduces the published eclipse duration, and its origin is unknown.
- For HD 80606 b the time of smallest projected separation is 11.4 min before conjunction. A mid-time measured from the symmetry of a light curve is closer to the midpoint of the contacts than to conjunction; the three should not be mixed for inclined eccentric orbits ([Validation](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#orbit-midtransit)).
- Orbits are fixed Keplerian ellipses: no apsidal or nodal precession, no light-travel-time correction of transit times, no relativistic terms. Mutual perturbations need the [N-body](#nbody) option.

References: [Danby 1987](#ref-danby1987); [Winn 2010](#ref-winn2010); [Pearson et al. 2022](#ref-pearson2022).

## 5. Radial velocities

Code: `src/core/rv.js`, `src/core/model.js`

The velocity of the star in dataset $d$ at time $t$ is

$$
v_d(t) = \gamma_d + \sum_p K_p \left[\cos(\omega_p + \nu_p(t)) + e_p \cos\omega_p\right] + c_1 (t - t_\mathrm{ref}) + c_2 (t - t_\mathrm{ref})^2
$$

$$
K = \left(\frac{2\pi G}{P}\right)^{1/3} \frac{M_p \sin i}{(M_\star + M_p)^{2/3}\sqrt{1 - e^2}}
$$

with the same orbit as the transit model, so the star recedes before mid-transit and approaches after it. $t_\mathrm{ref}$ is the earliest velocity. A planet's amplitude is computed from its mass (the sampled parameter is $M_p$ in Jupiter masses), or $K$ can be given directly. $\gamma_d$ is the zero point of instrument $d$ and is integrated out analytically (see [The likelihood](#likelihood)); each instrument also has a jitter $s_d$ added in quadrature to its uncertainties. $c_1$ and $c_2$ (keys `rvlin`, `rvquad`) are shared by all instruments. The inverse (mass from $K$) is solved by fixed-point iteration.

### Where the semi-amplitude comes from

Momentum about the barycentre: the star and the planet move on similar ellipses about their common centre of mass, $M_\star a_\star = M_p a_p$, so the star's semi-major axis is a fraction of the relative orbit's $a = a_\star + a_p$:

$$
a_\star = a\,\frac{M_p}{M_\star + M_p}
$$

A Keplerian orbit seen at inclination $i$ moves the star along the line of sight at $v_r = K\left[\cos(\omega + \nu) + e\cos\omega\right]$, with $K$ the orbital speed scale of the star times $\sin i$ (from $r = a_\star(1 - e^2)/(1 + e\cos\nu)$ and the constant specific angular momentum $r^2\dot\nu = 2\pi a_\star^2\sqrt{1 - e^2}/P$):

$$
K = \frac{2\pi}{P}\,\frac{a_\star \sin i}{\sqrt{1 - e^2}}
$$

Kepler's third law for the relative orbit gives $a$ from the period and the total mass:

$$
a^3 = \frac{G\,(M_\star + M_p)\,P^2}{4\pi^2}
$$

Putting the three together, $\frac{2\pi}{P}\left[\frac{G (M_\star + M_p) P^2}{4\pi^2}\right]^{1/3} = \left[\frac{2\pi G (M_\star + M_p)}{P}\right]^{1/3}$, and multiplying by $M_p/(M_\star + M_p)$ leaves $(M_\star + M_p)^{1/3 - 1} = (M_\star + M_p)^{-2/3}$: the equation above. `src/core/rv.js` \`semiAmplitude\` evaluates it with the IAU nominal $G M_\odot$ and the Jupiter-to-Sun mass ratio; \`massFromK\` inverts it by iteration, because $M_p$ appears on both sides.

### Accuracy and checks

- Velocity curves of 5 orbits up to $e$ = 0.93 against 30-digit arithmetic: worst 1.3e-14 $K$; $K$ from the masses against the two-body formula with IAU nominal constants: 3.1e-8 relative (`node test/validation.test.mjs`; [Validation: the star's velocity](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-rv)).
- HD 80606 b, velocities from seven instruments: K = 469.6 m/s (published 469.2, EXOTIC 469.9). ([Validation: EXOTIC’s own examples, reproduced](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-exotic); `test/exotic.test.mjs`)
- Velocity semi-amplitude of Jupiter and Earth against astropy constants: 12.474 and 0.08947 m/s in both. ([Validation: Estimates in the catalogue](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-relations); `test/relations.test.mjs`)

### Assumptions and limits

- The reflex motion uses the two-body factor $M_p/(M_\star + M_p)$. EXOTIC scales by $M_p/M_\star$, so for the same velocities the mass from this code is higher by $M_p/M_\star$ (0.38% for HD 80606 b).
- Not modelled: stellar activity (no Gaussian process or activity indicators in the likelihood), light-travel time, instrument-specific trends. The jitter is white. The Rossiter-McLaughlin anomaly is optional ([Rossiter-McLaughlin effect](#rm)).
- Stellar mass (and radius, when $a/R_\star$ follows from Kepler's law) are held at their input values unless made free; the uncertainty of a planet mass then does not include that of the stellar mass, and the Results tab says so.
- For the HD 80606 velocities $\chi^2$ = 1555 for 264 points with the jitters at zero (stored result `public/examples/results/hd80606-rv.json`), so formal uncertainties from that fit are too small unless the jitters are freed.

References: [Fulton et al. 2018](#ref-fulton2018); [Pearson et al. 2022](#ref-pearson2022); [Zellem et al. 2020](#ref-zellem2020).

<a id="rm"></a>

## 6. Rossiter-McLaughlin effect

Code: `src/core/rm.js`, `src/core/model.js (buildProblem)`

When `vsini` is set, every planet in front of the star adds to the velocities the shift of the flux-weighted mean velocity of the light that is not covered. The star rotates as a solid body; in the sky frame of the orbit (planet moving toward $+X$ across the disc, the orbit normal projected onto $+Y$, the chord at $Y = -b$) a point of the disc recedes at

$$
v(x, y) = v\sin i_\star\,(x\cos\lambda - y\sin\lambda)
$$

with $\lambda$ the sky-projected obliquity, the angle from the projected orbit normal to the projected stellar spin (ellc's convention [Maxted 2016](#ref-maxted2016); $\lambda = 0$ aligned, $180^\circ$ retrograde). With the Claret-law intensity $I$ of the fit's limb darkening (or another law given for the spectrograph's band through `spec.rm`) the anomaly is

$$
\Delta v = -\frac{\int_\mathrm{occ} I\,v\,dA}{F_\star - \int_\mathrm{occ} I\,dA}
$$

the quantity Ohta et al. expand for a small planet [Ohta, Taruya & Suto 2005](#ref-ohta2005). The integral over the occulted area is not approximated: the first moment $\int_\mathrm{occ} I\,x'\,dA$ along the line from the star's centre to the planet's is a line integral of $F(r) = \int_0^r I r\,dr$ (the closed form of the transit model) around the occulted region, an arc of the planet's limb with 40 Gauss-Legendre nodes plus, in ingress and egress, an arc of the stellar limb; the moment perpendicular to that line vanishes by symmetry. The blocked flux is the transit model's. Each planet has its own $\lambda$ (key `lambda@c`, falling back to `lambda`); the star's `vsini` is in km/s.

### What a Gaussian fit to the CCF measures (option)

With `spec.rm.method` = 'ccf' the anomaly is instead the shift of the centre of a Gaussian fitted to the cross-correlation function. Every surface element contributes a Gaussian line of dispersion $\beta_p$ (instrumental and thermal, `beta`; macroturbulence `zeta` adds $\zeta^2/2$ to $\beta_p^2$, a Gaussian approximation), the occulted light is a fraction $f$ with mean velocity $v_p$ (both from the integrals above), and to first order in $f$ the linearised least-squares fit moves by

$$
\Delta v = -\frac{f}{1 - f}\,g\,v_p\left(\frac{2\beta_0^2}{\beta_0^2 + \beta_p^2}\right)^{3/2}\exp\left(-\frac{v_p^2}{2(\beta_0^2 + \beta_p^2)}\right)
$$

[Hirano et al. 2010](#ref-hirano2010); [Boué et al. 2013](#ref-boue2013), with $\beta_0$ the dispersion of the out-of-transit CCF (measured, `beta0`, or that of the Gaussian that best fits the modelled rotation-broadened profile) and $g$ the correction for a profile that is not Gaussian (its area over the fitted Gaussian's, and the curvature term the out-of-transit residual leaves in the Hessian): 1.000 for $v\sin i/\beta_p$ = 0.57, 0.974 for 4. Both are tabulated against $v\sin i/\beta_p$ once per fit.

### Exposures, limb darkening, priors (options)

Each velocity dataset may carry its exposure (`exposure_min`; or `spec.rm.exptime` for all), over which the anomaly is averaged with `supersample` sub-samples (default 5); the Keplerian part is not averaged. The limb darkening of the anomaly is the spectrograph's band when `spec.rm.ld` is given. A catalogue $v\sin i_\star$ enters as a normal prior truncated at zero (vsiniPrior). The true obliquity follows from $\cos\psi = \cos i_\star\cos i + \sin i_\star\sin i\cos\lambda$ when $i_\star$ is known.

### Accuracy and checks

- Against a brute-force pixel sum (4000 × 4000 pixels over the planet's disc, star flux by scipy quadrature; `test/make_rm_reference.py`): 160 cases (uniform, quadratic and four-coefficient laws, $k$ = 0.01 to 0.2, inside the disc, on the limb, in ingress and egress, four obliquities), largest difference 1.0e-7 $v\sin i$ or 8.9 ppm of the anomaly, every case within the pixel sum's own error (`node test/rm.test.mjs`).
- Uniform star with the planet on the disc against $\Delta v = -v\sin i\,x_s k^2/(1 - k^2)$: 3.5e-18. The small-planet limit of Ohta et al. [Ohta, Taruya & Suto 2005](#ref-ohta2005): relative difference 8.0e-4, 8.8e-5 and 7.9e-6 at $k$ = 0.03, 0.01, 0.003, falling as $k^2$.
- CCF form against a brute-force disc integration (3000 × 3000 pixels of the star, 700 × 700 of the planet, each a Gaussian line, binned in velocity) with Gaussians fitted by scipy to the out-of-transit and in-transit profiles (`test/make_rm_ccf_reference.py`; 120 cases: $v\sin i$ = 1.7 to 12 km/s with $\beta$ = 3 km/s, and 5 km/s with $\beta$ = 2.5, $\zeta$ = 4 km/s; $\lambda$ = 0°, 40°; $k$ = 0.05, 0.1; six positions): $\beta_0$ within 1.7e-4, the anomaly within 0.14% of its largest value at $v\sin i/\beta$ = 0.57, 0.38% at 1, 0.93% at 2, 1.48% at 4. The first moment misses the fitted centre by 2.6%, 7.4%, 21% and 35% at those ratios. Exposure averaging (20 min, 7 sub-samples) is within 0.051 m/s of a 4001-point average where the exposure changes the anomaly by 4.05 m/s (`node test/rmccf.test.mjs`).
- HD 80606 b from the bundled velocities (SOPHIE 2009 February 14, 48 points of which 28 in transit; HIRES 2009 June 5, 12 and 8), orbit of the stored joint fit with $k$ = 0.1001 (Winn et al. 2009; the TESS curve is diluted by HD 80607), limb darkening of 390 to 690 nm: $v\sin i$ = 1.47 +0.22 −0.17 km/s and $\lambda$ = 58 +16 −12° with the orbit fixed, 1.49 +0.22 −0.17 km/s and 57 +17 −12° with $P$, $T_0$, $e$, $\omega$, $M_p$ free under the joint posterior, 1.47 and 57° with the CCF form ($\beta$ = 3 km/s) and 10-minute exposures. Hébrard et al. 2010 give $\lambda$ = 42 ± 8° and $v\sin i$ ≈ 1.7 km/s from the full transit of 2010 January, which is not in this file (1.1σ and 0.6σ away); Winn et al. 2009 give 50 +61 −36° from the HIRES night (`node test/hd80606rm.test.mjs`).
- Whole curves from the orbit against ellc's flux-weighted velocities [Maxted 2016](#ref-maxted2016) (`test/make_rm_ellc_reference.py`; $a/R_\star$ = 10, $k$ = 0.1, $v\sin i$ = 5 km/s, $\lambda$ = 0°, 30°, −45°, 120° at $i$ = 87° and 89.5°): at most 0.026 m/s of 23 to 39 m/s; the opposite sign of $\lambda$ misses by at least 5.3 m/s. A fit to 70 simulated in-transit velocities (2 m/s) returns $v\sin i$ = 4.97 ± 0.09 km/s (5) and $\lambda$ = 30.0 ± 1.0° (30).

### Assumptions and limits

- By default the anomaly is the first moment of the uncovered light, which is what iodine-cell velocities approximate; the CCF form is an option for the whole fit (not per dataset), first order in the occulted fraction, with Gaussian local lines and a Gaussian macroturbulence (Hirano et al. 2011's radial-tangential profile is not implemented), and its $\beta_0$ depends on the velocity window of the fit (here $\pm(v\sin i + 6\beta_p)$) unless the measured one is given.
- Solid-body rotation, no differential rotation or convective blueshift; the planet is dark (its own light and a moon are not in the anomaly); planets are added independently (no overlap of two planets on the disc).
- With N-body dynamics the anomaly uses the Keplerian sky positions. Exposure averaging applies to the anomaly only.

References: [Ohta, Taruya & Suto 2005](#ref-ohta2005); [Maxted 2016](#ref-maxted2016); [Hirano et al. 2010](#ref-hirano2010); [Boué et al. 2013](#ref-boue2013).

<a id="likelihood"></a>

## 7. The likelihood

Code: `src/core/model.js (buildProblem)`, `src/core/priors.js`, `src/main.js (defaultPrior)`

There is one likelihood, `buildProblem`. It is the sum of independent Gaussian terms for the light curve(s), the velocities and the event times, each with its normalisation, so that the evidence is a normalised marginal likelihood.

### Light curves

A dataset holds one or more epochs $s$ (nights, visits, orbits). The model for point $i$ of epoch $s$ is $a_s\,m_i$ with

$$
m_i = e^{\kappa_s X_i} \prod_p f_p(t_i)
$$

where $f_p$ is planet $p$'s (exposure-averaged) transit flux, $X_i$ the airmass and $\kappa_s$ the airmass coefficient of the epoch (absent without an airmass column). The normalisation $a_s$ enters linearly and is integrated out analytically with a uniform prior $a_s \sim U(0, 2)$ instead of being sampled:

$$
\ln L_s = -\frac{1}{2}\chi^2_{s,\min} + \frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{2\pi}{\sum_i m_i^2/\sigma_i^2} - \ln 2 - \frac{1}{2}\sum_i \ln(2\pi\sigma_i^2), \qquad \chi^2_{s,\min} = \sum_i \frac{d_i^2}{\sigma_i^2} - \frac{\left(\sum_i d_i m_i/\sigma_i^2\right)^2}{\sum_i m_i^2/\sigma_i^2}
$$

The Gaussian integral over $a_s$ is taken over the whole real line, which is exact to the extent that the conditional posterior of $a_s$ lies well inside (0, 2); the reader divides fluxes by their median when it is more than 2% from 1 (and always for magnitudes). The conditional best value $\hat{a}_s = \sum d_i m_i/\sigma_i^2 \,/ \sum m_i^2/\sigma_i^2$ is the weighted least-squares amplitude and is what the plots show.

`buildProblem` also accepts linear regressors $x_k$ per point (a slope in time, a centroid): the baseline of epoch $s$ becomes $e^{\kappa_s X}(a_s + \sum_k c_{sk} x_k)$ and all $p$ linear coefficients are integrated out together, with $c_{sk} \sim U(-1, 1)$:

$$
\ln L_s = -\frac{1}{2}\chi^2_{s,\min} + \frac{1}{2}\left(p \ln 2\pi - \ln\det A\right) - p\ln 2 - \frac{1}{2}\sum_i \ln(2\pi\sigma_i^2), \qquad A = G^{T} W G
$$

where the columns of $G$ are the model times $(1, x_1, \ldots)$. A session stores the detector columns and the detrending choice (`docs/FORMAT.md`), and `specFromSession` rebuilds the regressors (or the kernel) from them exactly as the analyzer does, so a session re-run headlessly or from Python is fitted with its systematics model.

### Light-curve jitter and dilution

An optional white-noise jitter $j_s$ per epoch (key `jitlc`, or `jitlc@2` for the second epoch; in ppm) is added in quadrature, $\sigma_i^2 = e_i^2 + j_s^2$, everywhere above: in the weights and in $-\frac{1}{2}\sum_i \ln(2\pi\sigma_i^2)$, which is what stops a free jitter from growing without bound. For the information criteria $\chi^2$ is replaced by $\chi^2 + \sum_i \ln(\sigma_i^2/e_i^2)$, as for the velocity jitter.

Dilution (third light) by other stars in the aperture: with $d$ the ratio of their flux to the target's (key `dil`, per epoch `dil@2`), the astrophysical model is replaced by

$$
m_i \to \frac{m_i + d}{1 + d}
$$

before the airmass term, the regressors and the kernel, so it is still 1 out of transit and every depth is divided by $1 + d$. A contamination fraction $D$ of the light in the aperture (TESS's CROWDSAP is $1 - D$) is $d = D/(1 - D)$. Without a measurement of $d$ (photometry of the neighbour, a second band) it is degenerate with $k$ and should be fixed or given a prior.

### Velocities

For dataset $d$ with residuals $r_i = v_i - v_\mathrm{model}(t_i)$ (model without $\gamma_d$), variances $\sigma_i^2 + s_d^2$, weights $w_i = 1/(\sigma_i^2 + s_d^2)$ and $\gamma_d \sim U(-10^5, 10^5)$ m/s integrated out:

$$
\ln L_d = -\frac{1}{2}\left[\sum_i w_i r_i^2 - \frac{(\sum_i w_i r_i)^2}{\sum_i w_i}\right] - \frac{1}{2}\sum_i \ln\!\left[2\pi(\sigma_i^2 + s_d^2)\right] + \frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{2\pi}{\sum_i w_i} - \ln(2\times10^5)
$$

The $\ln(\sigma^2 + s^2)$ term is what keeps a free jitter from growing without bound.

### Event times

Mid-transit times of a planet are compared with $T_0 + E P$ and mid-eclipse times with the superior conjunction plus $E P$, $E$ being the nearest whole orbit; an optional timing noise $\sigma_t$ is added in quadrature:

$$
\ln L_\mathrm{tim} = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_i \left[\frac{(t_i - T_0 - E_i P)^2}{\sigma_i^2 + \sigma_t^2} + \ln 2\pi(\sigma_i^2 + \sigma_t^2)\right]
$$

### Prior support

A point is rejected ($\ln L = -10^{100}$) when $e \notin [0, 0.999)$, $P \le 0$, $(a/R_\star)(1 - e) \le 1$, $k \le 0$, $M_p < 0$, a jitter is negative, the limb-darkening profile is not physical, or an optional model reports an impossible configuration. Priors are uniform or normal (truncated normal and log-uniform exist for programmatic use), applied as transforms of the unit cube.

### Default priors in the analyzer

These are starting points computed from the current value $v$ of each parameter (`defaultPrior` in `src/main.js`); every prior is shown and editable on the Fit tab and is written into the session and the exported script. Report the priors you used.

| Parameter | Default prior |
| --- | --- |
| $R_p/R_\star$ | $U(\max(0.001, 0.5v),\ \min(0.6, 1.6v))$ |
| $i$ | $U(\max(60^\circ, v - 5^\circ),\ 90^\circ)$ |
| $P$ | one light curve: $N(v,\ \max(10^{-6}, 10^{-5}v))$ d; several epochs: $U$ about $v$ wide enough to move the last transit by a quarter of $T_{14}$ relative to the first |
| $T_0$ | $U(v \pm \max(0.01,\ 0.2\,T_{14}))$ d |
| $e$ | $U(0,\ \min(0.95, \max(0.3, v + 0.2)))$ |
| $\omega$ | $U(v \pm 30^\circ)$ |
| $M_p$ | $U(0,\ \max(5v, 0.02))\ M_\mathrm{Jup}$ |
| limb darkening | $U(v \pm 0.3)$ per coefficient; $q_1, q_2 \sim U(0, 1)$ |
| airmass coefficient $\kappa$ | $U(-0.2, 0.2)$ |
| velocity trend | $c_1 \sim U(-0.1, 0.1)$ m/s/d; $c_2 \sim U(-10^{-3}, 10^{-3})$ m/s/d² |
| jitter | $U(0,\ \max(15, 5\times\text{median } \sigma))$ m/s |
| light-curve jitter | $U(0,\ \max(500, 3\times\text{median } \sigma))$ ppm |
| dilution $d$ | $U(0,\ \max(1, 3v))$; not ticked when added |
| $v\sin i_\star$, $\lambda$ | $U(0,\ \max(20, 3v))$ km/s; $U(-180^\circ, 180^\circ)$ |
| $M_\star$, $R_\star$ | $N(v, \sigma)$ with the catalogue uncertainty, or 5% of the value |
| $T_\mathrm{eff}$, [Fe/H] | $N(v, \sigma)$ with the catalogue uncertainty, or 100 K and 0.1 dex |
| planet's light | $F_p/F_\star \sim U(0, \max(0.05, 3v))$; contrast $U(0, 1)$; hot-spot offset $U(-90^\circ, 90^\circ)$; second harmonic $U(-0.25, 0.25)$; ellipsoidal $U(0, 500)$ ppm; beaming $U(-50, 50)$ ppm; map coefficients $U(-0.6, 0.6)$ for degree 1, $U(-0.3, 0.3)$ above |
| moon | $R_m/R_\star \sim U(0, \max(0.05, 2.5v))$; period $U(0.97v, 1.03v)$; phase $U(0, 1)$; mass ratio $U(0, 0.1)$; tilt $U(0^\circ, 60^\circ)$ |

A look-up in the catalogue suggests wider priors from the published uncertainties (`suggestPriors`: for example $R_p/R_\star$ uniform within $\pm\max(10\sigma, 0.5k)$, $P$ normal with $\max(5\sigma, 10^{-5}P)$, $T_0$ uniform within $\pm\max(10\sqrt{\sigma_{T}^2 + (N\sigma_P)^2},\ 0.5\,T_{14},\ 0.02\,\mathrm{d})$). The Fit tab's "EXOTIC's bounds" preset sets $R_p/R_\star \in [0, 1.25v]$, $i \pm 5^\circ$, $T_0$ within a quarter orbit and the airmass coefficient in $[-3, 3]$.

### Information criteria

$\mathrm{BIC} = \chi^2 + k\ln n$ [Schwarz 1978](#ref-schwarz1978), $\mathrm{AIC} = \chi^2 + 2k$ and $\chi^2/(n - k)$ are reported at the best-fitting point, with $k$ the number of sampled parameters plus the analytically integrated ones (one normalisation per epoch, one zero point per velocity dataset) and $n$ the number of measurements of every kind.

### Accuracy and checks

- Several nights in one fit: ln L against quadrature over each normalisation: difference 9.5e-8 at ln L = 2468.49. ([Validation: Evidence, ephemerides and geometry](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-basics); `test/multiepoch.test.mjs`)
- ln Z against midpoint quadrature, three free parameters: quadrature 1640.001; sampler mean of six seeds within its reported error. ([Validation: Evidence, ephemerides and geometry](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-basics); `test/evidence.test.mjs`)
- Light-curve jitter and dilution: $\ln L$ of a two-epoch light curve at four values of the jitters and $d$ against the integral over $a_s$ done numerically (scipy quad; `test/make_lcnoise_reference.py`): largest difference 1.2e-6; maximum-likelihood jitters 1470.71 and 617.61 ppm against scipy's 1470.70 and 617.57; injected 1500 and 600 ppm recovered as 1489 +107 −101 and 592 +110 −120; every point of a limb-darkened, exposure-averaged transit obeys depth$(d)$ = depth$(0)/(1 + d)$ to 1.6e-16; a fit without the correction returns $k/\sqrt{1 + d}$ (`node test/lcnoise.test.mjs`).
- Detrending in sessions: the regressors `specFromSession` builds equal the centroids standardised by hand plus a Legendre $P_1(t)$, the likelihood equals the analyzer's import path exactly, and `runSession` recovers $k$ = 0.1006 ± 0.0005 (0.1) where the same session without its systematics model gives 0.1124 ± 0.0003 (`node test/sessiondetrend.test.mjs`; the Python package gives the Node $\chi^2$ to 1e-12, `python/tests/test_detrend.py`).
- $\ln L$ against an independent Python implementation whose models come from exoplanet-core and radvel: largest difference 3.8e-6 over 24 points in four problems (`node test/validation.test.mjs`).
- Three-planet toy system: χ² of each light curve at the injected values: 45.11, 88.80 and 190.58 in both codes. ([Validation: EXOTIC’s own examples, reproduced](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-exotic); `test/exotic.test.mjs`)

### Assumptions and limits

- The noise model is white and Gaussian: the uncertainties as given, plus the optional light-curve jitter. There is no correlated-noise term in the likelihood and no outlier model. Underestimated error bars without a jitter give posteriors that are too narrow and exaggerate every evidence difference.
- Detrending is a multiplicative $e^{\kappa X}$ airmass term per epoch plus, when the light curve carries detector columns, linear regressors or a kernel model. Space-based systematics without such columns must be removed before the fit; the phase-curve examples use data detrended elsewhere.
- All epochs share one $T_0$ and $P$ (no per-epoch mid-times in a joint fit), one exposure model per epoch and one limb-darkening band.
- With several planets the light curve is the product of the planets' fluxes: planet-planet occultations during simultaneous transits are not modelled, and when planets have their own light the star's light is counted twice at the 1e-6 level.

References: [Schwarz 1978](#ref-schwarz1978); [Zellem et al. 2020](#ref-zellem2020).

<a id="sampler"></a>

## 8. Nested sampling

Code: `src/core/nested.js (MiniNest)`, `src/core/fitRunner.js`, `src/core/stats.js`

Posteriors and the evidence $Z = \int L(\theta)\,\pi(\theta)\,d\theta$ are computed by nested sampling [Skilling 2006](#ref-skilling2006) with a sampler written for this project, `MiniNest`, which follows the strategy of UltraNest [Buchner 2021](#ref-buchner2021). Parameters are sampled in the unit cube and mapped through the inverse cumulative distribution of each prior.

### Algorithm

- **Live points.** $N = \max(400, 2d + 10)$ by default for $d$ free parameters, drawn uniformly in the unit cube.
- **Shrinkage.** At each iteration the live point of lowest likelihood $L_i$ is retired with weight $w_i = X_{i-1}\,(1 - e^{-1/N})$ and the prior volume shrinks as $\ln X_i = \ln X_{i-1} - 1/N$; then $Z = \sum_i L_i w_i$ plus the remaining live points, each with weight $X/N$. Live points with exactly equal likelihood (plateaus) are retired together with the volume rule of [Fowlie, Handley & Su 2021](#ref-fowlie2021).
- **Region.** New points are drawn uniformly from the MLFriends region [Buchner 2016](#ref-buchner2016); [Buchner 2019](#ref-buchner2019): live points are whitened, $t = A^{-1}(u - \bar{u})$ with $AA^{T}$ the covariance of the live points about the mean of their own cluster; the region is the union of balls of radius $r$ around the live points, intersected with an ellipsoid $|t|^2 \le R^2$ and the unit cube. $r$ is the largest distance from a left-out point to its nearest selected neighbour over 20 bootstrap rounds; the ellipsoid is enlarged by the largest ratio found when it is re-fitted to each bootstrap sample (UltraNest keeps the shape fixed, which biased $\ln Z$ upward with dimension in our tests). Clusters are found by linking points closer than $r$. The region is rebuilt after every $\max(20, N/5)$ replacements and its volume is not allowed to grow.
- **Slice sampling.** When drawing from the region costs more than three times a slice-sampled point (measured in likelihood calls), the sampler switches to slice sampling [Neal 2003](#ref-neal2003) from a random live point: $\max(10, 2d)$ steps, each along either the difference of two live points of the same cluster or a random direction in the whitened space, with a bracket from the ellipsoid chord or from stepping out, and shrinkage on rejection. It switches back when the region costs less than 1.5 times a slice point.
- **Self-test.** The rank at which each new point enters the live set must be uniform [Buchner 2016](#ref-buchner2016); [Buchner 2023](#ref-buchner2023). A Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of the ranks of region-drawn points is made after each rebuild (threshold $p < 10^{-5}$, at least 600 ranks) and at termination ($p < 10^{-3}$). On failure the region is no longer trusted: the sampler continues in slice mode and, if less than 30% of the budget is spent, restarts from fresh prior draws.
- **Termination.** The run stops as converged when the live points can hold less than a fraction $f$ of the evidence, $L_{\max} X / (Z + L_{\max} X) < f$, with $f$ = 0.01 by default. It also stops at a budget of likelihood calls (default 10⁶) or seconds; such a run returns what it has with `converged: false`.

### Uncertainty of the evidence

The volumes are random: each shrinkage factor is distributed as $\mathrm{Beta}(n_i, 1)$, $n_i$ being the number of live points at step $i$. $\ln Z$ is recomputed for 200 simulated sequences $X_{i+1} = X_i\,U^{1/n_i}$ (fixed seed) and its standard deviation taken; terms for plateaus, for the scatter of the final live points, and, in an unconverged run, half the range the remaining live points could add, are added in quadrature. The information $H$ and the effective sample size $(\sum w)^2/\sum w^2$ are reported with it.

### Posterior summaries

The result is a weighted sample. Reported values are weighted medians with the 15.87% and 84.13% quantiles (no interpolation between sample points). Equal-weight draws for plots, derived quantities and stored posteriors are made by systematic resampling with a fixed seed.

### Warnings

The sampler writes warnings in plain words: not converged (with the fraction of evidence still in the live points); fewer than 150 effective samples; sampling efficiency below 1%; a failed insertion-order test and whether the run restarted; more than half of the points from slice sampling; a posterior piled against an edge of its prior, or equal to its prior; separate peaks with their weights; pairs of parameters correlated above 0.95, with advice. They are stored in the session and belong in a paper's description of the fit when present.

### Reproducibility

The random-number generator is sfc32 seeded from the session (seed 42 by default). For a given seed a run is the same every time on the same JavaScript engine; only the optional time limit depends on the clock.

### What the evidence can and cannot be used for

$\ln Z$ is a normalised marginal likelihood: the Gaussian normalisations are included, the priors are proper, and the analytically integrated parameters carry their prior widths. It can therefore be compared between models **fitted to the same data with the same error bars**, when both runs converged. It cannot be used: across different data or error bars; from an unconverged run (it is then a lower limit); between an N-body fit with the profiled straight line and a Keplerian fit; or without regard to the priors, since widening a prior on a constrained parameter lowers $\ln Z$ by the logarithm of the factor. Its quoted uncertainty is the sampling error only.

### Accuracy and checks

- Correlated Gaussian, 10 parameters, ρ = 0.99: ln Z = −7.729 ± 0.335, exact −6.931 (2.4σ low on this seed; over 32 seeds the mean offset is −0.078 ± 0.054). ([Validation: The nested sampler on hard problems](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-sampler); `test/stress.test.mjs`)
- Transit with a/R★ and inclination both free (0.99 correlated): ln Z = 744.121 ± 0.196, quadrature 744.090; means within 0.025 sd. ([Validation: The nested sampler on hard problems](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-sampler); `test/stress.test.mjs`)
- Period aliases: three separate peaks: ln Z = 2.166 ± 0.154, exact 2.121; the peaks are reported with their weights. ([Validation: The nested sampler on hard problems](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-sampler); `test/stress.test.mjs`)
- Neal’s funnel, 4 parameters: ln Z = −16.872 ± 0.158, exact −16.588 (1.8σ low on this seed); over 48 seeds −0.045 ± 0.026 since the ellipsoid check, −0.24 ± 0.05 before. ([Validation: The nested sampler on hard problems](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-sampler); `test/stress.test.mjs`)
- Correlated Gaussian, 15 parameters, ρ = 0.99: ln Z = −10.245 ± 0.359, exact −10.397. ([Validation: The nested sampler on hard problems](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-sampler); `test/stress.test.mjs`)
- Banana, 5 parameters: ln Z = −17.033 ± 0.204, exact −16.732 (1.5σ); posterior widths off by 23% on this seed, beyond the 20% tolerance. ([Validation: The nested sampler on hard problems](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-sampler); `test/stress.test.mjs`)
- ln Z against midpoint quadrature, three free parameters: quadrature 1640.001; sampler mean of six seeds within its reported error. ([Validation: Evidence, ephemerides and geometry](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-basics); `test/evidence.test.mjs`)
- Four simulated problems against dynesty (3000 live points), UltraNest and emcee on an independent Python likelihood (`node test/validation.test.mjs`): posterior means within 0.04σ and widths within 3.5%; $\ln Z$ within 0.31 (1.5 combined σ) of dynesty and UltraNest; over eight seeds the mean $\ln Z$ is within 0.09 of the reference and its scatter between seeds (0.07 to 0.21) is no larger than about the reported error (0.12 to 0.20). [Validation: fits and their error bars](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-fits).
- Coverage, 300 simulated data sets each: the truth lies inside the 68% interval in 67.0 to 68.0% of transit fits and 69.0 to 73.3% of velocity fits (expected 68 ± 2.7%; the velocity amplitude and $\omega$ are 2σ high), and inside the 95% interval in 94.0 to 96.7% (same test). The data are simulated with this code's own model and white noise, so this tests the sampler and the likelihood, not the model.

### Assumptions and limits

- Funnel-shaped posteriors bias the evidence low by a few tenths, sometimes without a warning; the project's notes record 0.5 to 0.9 on some seeds.
- In slice mode the scatter of $\ln Z$ between runs exceeds the quoted error (rms pull up to 1.9 in the stress suite).
- In the stored run of `test/nested.test.mjs` an 8-dimensional correlated Gaussian gives $\ln Z$ = −23.357 ± 0.274 against the exact −23.966, that is 0.61 (2.2 reported σ) high; the 2- and 5-dimensional cases are within 1σ.
- A mode much narrower than another can be lost. Twenty parameters with correlations of 0.999 do not converge within the default budget (reported as such).
- A run stopped early has an effective sample size near 1; its intervals mean nothing, and the Results tab says so instead of showing them.
- Not implemented: a variable number of live points, a separate metric per mode, warm starts, resuming from disk.
- Coverage has been verified only on data simulated by this code's model with white noise. Correlated noise and model misspecification are untested.

References: [Skilling 2006](#ref-skilling2006); [Buchner 2016](#ref-buchner2016); [Buchner 2019](#ref-buchner2019); [Buchner 2021](#ref-buchner2021); [Buchner 2023](#ref-buchner2023); [Neal 2003](#ref-neal2003); [Fowlie, Handley & Su 2021](#ref-fowlie2021); [Speagle 2020](#ref-speagle2020); [Foreman-Mackey et al. 2013](#ref-foremanmackey2013).

<a id="comparison"></a>

## 9. Model comparison and its cautions

Code: `src/main.js (readBayes, runAlarms)`, `src/core/model.js (infoCriteria)`

The Results tab keeps every run on the same data and compares them by $\Delta\ln Z$, the logarithm of the Bayes factor [Kass & Raftery 1995](#ref-kass1995), against the run with the highest evidence. The thresholds 2.5 and 5 (odds of about 12 and 150 to 1) are the scale of [Trotta 2008](#ref-trotta2008), an adaptation of Jeffreys' scale; the requirement that a difference also exceed 1 and twice its uncertainty is the software's own, deliberately conservative. With $\sigma_\Delta$ the quadrature sum of the two evidence uncertainties,

| Condition | Reading |
| --- | --- |
| either run not converged | not comparable |
| $\|\Delta\ln Z\| < \max(1, 2\sigma_\Delta)$ | indistinguishable |
| up to 2.5 | weakly disfavoured |
| 2.5 to 5 (odds of about 12 to 150) | moderately disfavoured |
| above 5 | strongly disfavoured |

Runs on other data are hidden from the comparison. Each run also lists reasons not to trust its evidence: not converged; fewer than 200 effective samples; insertion-order test with $p < 0.01$; $\chi^2/N$ above 1.6 (error bars too small or model incomplete, which exaggerates every $\Delta\ln Z$) or below 0.5; sampler warnings; priors on shared parameters that differ from the reference run (part of $\Delta\ln Z$ is then the change of prior volume); different kinds of data in the fit.

The Timing tab compares ephemeris models by $\mathrm{BIC} = \chi^2 + k\ln n$ [Schwarz 1978](#ref-schwarz1978) and describes a difference above 2, 6 and 10 as positive, strong and very strong, the scale of [Kass & Raftery 1995](#ref-kass1995) for twice the log Bayes factor.

### Accuracy and checks

- `test/evidence.test.mjs` checks that a transit model is preferred over no transit on simulated data ($\Delta\ln Z$ = 6164.6 in the stored output); there is no test of model comparison between two close models.

### Assumptions and limits

- The evidence depends on the prior widths chosen. A model comparison in a paper should state the priors of both models and, ideally, show that the conclusion survives a reasonable change of them.
- The uncertainty of $\ln Z$ is sampling error. Systematic bias of the sampler (see [Nested sampling](#sampler)) is of the same size as the "indistinguishable" threshold; differences below about 1 should not be interpreted.
- The BIC is an approximation that ignores the priors. On signal-free timing lists the BIC alone prefers a sinusoid in 58% of cases (project notes), which is why the Timing tab also requires a significant periodogram peak.
- Both criteria assume the error bars are right. They are not rescaled during a fit. The Data tab's "Rescale errors" multiplies every error bar of an epoch by one factor $\beta_k = \sqrt{\chi^2_k / (n_k (N - k)/N)}$, with $k$ the free parameters plus one normalisation per epoch, so that $\chi^2/(N - k) = 1$ about the model on screen; the relative sizes of the error bars are kept (`test/data.test.mjs`).

References: [Kass & Raftery 1995](#ref-kass1995); [Trotta 2008](#ref-trotta2008); [Schwarz 1978](#ref-schwarz1978).

<a id="timing"></a>

## 10. Ephemerides, timing, periodograms and orbital decay

Code: `src/core/ephemeris.js`, `src/core/periodogram.js`, `src/ui/timingTab.js`

### Ephemerides

Mid-transit times $t_i \pm \sigma_i$ at whole-orbit epochs $E_i$ are fitted by weighted linear least squares with

$$
T(E) = T_0 + P E \qquad \text{or} \qquad T(E) = T_0 + P E + \frac{1}{2}\frac{dP}{dE}E^2, \qquad \frac{dP}{dt} = \frac{1}{P}\frac{dP}{dE}
$$

The fit is done in a centred, scaled epoch variable with a time offset removed, then mapped back to epoch 0, so Julian dates keep their precision. The covariance is $(G^{T} W G)^{-1}$ from the error bars as given; it is **not** rescaled by $\chi^2$, and the tab says so when $\chi^2/\mathrm{dof} > 2$. The uncertainty of a predicted time is $\sigma_T^2(E) = g^{T} C g$ with $g = (1, E, E^2)$ in the scaled variable, and $\sigma(dP/dt)$ includes the covariance with $P$. When a list has no epoch column, $E_i = \mathrm{round}[(t_i - t_\mathrm{ref})/P]$ with the system period; a time more than 0.2 periods from a whole orbit raises a warning. The quadratic term is the only decay model: it describes orbital decay, or apsidal precession to first order; there is no separate precession model. Linear and quadratic fits are compared by BIC.

### Periodic signals in the residuals

The residuals from the ephemeris are searched with the generalised Lomb-Scargle periodogram [Zechmeister & Kürster 2009](#ref-zechmeister2009) (weights $1/\sigma_i^2$, floating mean), in the normalisation $p(f) = 1 - \chi^2(f)/\chi^2_0$, where $\chi^2(f)$ is that of the best sinusoid plus constant at frequency $f$. Epochs are a lattice, so the shortest period searched is two lattice steps (a true Nyquist limit) and the longest twice the time span, on a grid oversampled 10 times. The false-alarm probability of the highest peak is the analytic bound of [Baluev 2008](#ref-baluev2008), $\mathrm{FAP} \approx 1 - (1 - \mathrm{FAP}_\mathrm{single})\,e^{-\tau(z)}$, as implemented in astropy [VanderPlas 2018](#ref-vanderplas2018); a bootstrap over the residuals (1000 resamples) is available on request. A sinusoid is then fitted to the times themselves together with the ephemeris (linear least squares with a Gauss-Newton refinement of the period), the periodogram of what is left is computed, and a second sinusoid is tried. A sinusoid is recommended only if its peak has FAP below 1% **and** it lowers the BIC.

### Accuracy and checks

- Ephemeris coefficients against exact rational arithmetic: within 1.8e-6 σ. ([Validation: Evidence, ephemerides and geometry](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-basics); `test/ephemeris.test.mjs`)
- Orbital decay of WASP-12 b from the published dP/dE: −30.74 ± 2.69 ms/yr here, −30.72 ± 2.67 published. ([Validation: Evidence, ephemerides and geometry](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-basics); `test/ephemeris.test.mjs`)
- Power, four normalisations: 20,788 values within 4.0e-11 of the peak. ([Validation: Periodic signals in transit timing](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-periodogram); `test/periodogram.test.mjs`)
- False-alarm probabilities (Baluev and three others): relative difference 1.4e-14. ([Validation: Periodic signals in transit timing](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-periodogram); `test/periodogram.test.mjs`)
- A 2-minute signal in 30 of 500 epochs: detected in 93% of 300 trials. ([Validation: Periodic signals in transit timing](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-periodogram); `test/periodogram.test.mjs`)
- Lists with no signal, 1000 trials: flagged at the 1% level in 1.00%. ([Validation: Periodic signals in transit timing](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-periodogram); `test/periodogram.test.mjs`)
- Error bars too small by 45 s of unmodelled scatter: the analytic test raises false alarms in 68% of lists, the bootstrap in 1%. ([Validation: Periodic signals in transit timing](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-periodogram); `test/periodogram.test.mjs`)
- Coverage of the ephemeris fit over 4000 noise realisations and the comparison with exact rational arithmetic: `node test/ephemeris.test.mjs`.

### Assumptions and limits

- No published list of mid-transit times has been fitted end to end and compared with its paper; only the conversion from $dP/dE$ to $dP/dt$ was (WASP-12 b, [Leonardi et al. 2024](#ref-leonardi2024)).
- The analytic false-alarm probability trusts the error bars: with errors underestimated by 45 s of unmodelled scatter it raises false alarms in 68% of signal-free lists, the bootstrap in 1% (stored test output). Use the bootstrap when $\chi^2/\mathrm{dof}$ of the ephemeris is well above 1.
- Times are taken as given, with no conversion between time standards; the calendar column of predicted transits reads the listed time as UTC.
- A periodic signal in transit times has many physical explanations; the periodogram gives a period and amplitude, not a companion. See [N-body dynamics](#nbody).

References: [Zechmeister & Kürster 2009](#ref-zechmeister2009); [Baluev 2008](#ref-baluev2008); [VanderPlas 2018](#ref-vanderplas2018); [Astropy Collaboration 2022](#ref-astropy2022); [Leonardi et al. 2024](#ref-leonardi2024); [Schwarz 1978](#ref-schwarz1978).

<a id="multiplanet"></a>

## 11. Several planets and Kepler-tied a/R★

Code: `src/core/model.js`, `src/core/rv.js (arsFromKepler)`

A fit can hold several planets. The first planet's parameters have plain keys (`per`, `rprs`); the others carry their letter (`per@c`). Limb darkening belongs to the star and is shared. The light curve is the product of the planets' fluxes, the velocity the sum of their reflex terms, and each planet's event times are compared with its own ephemeris.

$a/R_\star$ is **never a sampled parameter**. With the inclination free the two trade off through the impact parameter $b = (a/R_\star)\cos i$: a transit of fixed duration and depth can be reproduced along a ridge in the ($a/R_\star$, $i$) plane, which costs the sampler several times more likelihood calls and inflates the uncertainty of $i$ without adding information that the stellar density does not already give. $a/R_\star$ is therefore either held at its input value, or, with "a/R★ from Kepler's law", computed for every sample from

$$
\frac{a}{R_\star} = \frac{1}{R_\star}\left[\frac{G\,(M_\star + M_p)\,P^2}{4\pi^2}\right]^{1/3}
$$

so that the photometry, the velocities and the timing describe one orbit. $M_\star$ and $R_\star$ can then be free parameters with normal priors at their measured uncertainties, which propagates the stellar density uncertainty into $a/R_\star$, $b$ and the durations.

### Accuracy and checks

- Transit with a/R★ and inclination both free (0.99 correlated): ln Z = 744.121 ± 0.196, quadrature 744.090; means within 0.025 sd. ([Validation: The nested sampler on hard problems](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-sampler); `test/stress.test.mjs`)
- Three-planet toy system: χ² of each light curve at the injected values: 45.11, 88.80 and 190.58 in both codes. ([Validation: EXOTIC’s own examples, reproduced](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-exotic); `test/exotic.test.mjs`)
- HD 80606 b, light curve + velocities + timing, against Table 7 of Pearson et al. 2022: P within 5e-4 d, i within 0.03°, e within 0.001, K within 3 m/s. ([Validation: EXOTIC’s own examples, reproduced](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-exotic); `test/exotic.test.mjs`)
- Project notes (README, "The sampler"): a transit fit with both $a/R_\star$ and $i$ free needed 47,000 likelihood calls and gave $\sigma(i)$ = 0.84°, against 11,600 calls and 0.076° with $a/R_\star$ fixed. These two numbers are from a development run and are not asserted by a test.

### Assumptions and limits

- Holding $a/R_\star$ fixed without freeing the star understates the uncertainty of $i$, $b$ and the durations: the quoted intervals are conditional on that value. For publication, use Kepler's law with $M_\star$ and $R_\star$ free under their measured uncertainties, or state the value $a/R_\star$ was fixed at and its source.
- The stellar density implied by a transit is not fitted independently of $M_\star$ and $R_\star$; an inconsistent stellar density (blend, wrong star) shows only as a poor fit.
- Seventeen free parameters for three planets converge in about 950,000 likelihood calls, close to the default budget.

References: [Winn 2010](#ref-winn2010); [Seager & Mallén-Ornelas 2003](#ref-seager2003).

<a id="viability"></a>

## 12. Physical priors: stable orbits and period aliases

Code: `src/core/physical.js`, `src/core/aliases.js`, `src/core/model.js (spec.physical, nalias)`, `src/core/priors.js (categorical)`

Optional prior constraints, each off unless `spec.physical` switches it on, applied in the likelihood before any model is computed (a point that fails has zero prior mass). Semi-major axes come from Kepler's law with each planet's period and mass, masses from `mplanet` or from $K$. **crossing**: the radial ranges of adjacent orbits do not overlap, $a_2(1 - e_2) > a_1(1 + e_1)$. **hill**: Gladman's Hill stability of each adjacent pair on coplanar eccentric orbits [Gladman 1993](#ref-gladman1993),

$$
\mu^{-3}\left(\mu_1 + \frac{\mu_2}{\ell^2}\right)\left(\mu_1\gamma_1 + \mu_2\gamma_2\ell\right)^2 > 1 + 3^{4/3}\frac{\mu_1\mu_2}{\mu^{4/3}},\qquad \ell = \sqrt{a_2/a_1},\ \gamma_i = \sqrt{1 - e_i^2}
$$

which for circular orbits is a separation of $2\sqrt{3}$ mutual Hill radii $R_H = [(m_1 + m_2)/3M_\star]^{1/3}(a_1 + a_2)/2$. **hillSpacing**: every adjacent pair at least that many $R_H$ apart (about 10 for three or more planets to survive $10^8$ orbits [Chambers et al. 1996](#ref-chambers1996)). **amd**: AMD stability [Laskar & Petit 2017](#ref-laskar2017) with coplanar orbits, $C/\Lambda_\mathrm{out} < C_c(\alpha, \gamma)$ for each pair and $C/\Lambda_1 < 1$. **roche**: periastron outside the star and outside $f\,R_p\,(M_\star/M_p)^{1/3}$, $f$ = 2.16 (Rappaport et al. 2013). **megno**: a short integration of the variational equations [Cincotta & Simó 2000](#ref-cincotta2000) for each candidate (expensive).

A truncated prior changes the evidence. The sampler integrates $L\pi$ over the allowed region, so its $Z$ is that of "this prior and a viable system"; the evidence of the renormalised prior $\pi/V$ is $Z/V$, with $V$ the prior mass that passes, estimated from 20,000 prior draws and stored by runSession as `result.prior_volume` ($\ln V$, and $\ln Z - \ln V$). Use $\ln Z$ to compare viable models with each other; $\ln Z - \ln V$ always gains about $-\ln V$ when the data already sit in the allowed region.

### Period aliases

A planet seen in transits a span $S$ apart has $P = S/N$. aliasScan predicts every transit of each $N$ and drops an $N$ that puts a transit inside covered data (more than half of its $T_{14}$ window observed) more than 0.1 d from every one seen, the rule of the owner's EXOTIC analysis of TOI-1873. The survivors go to the sampler as one categorical parameter `nalias` with `palias` = $S$, $P$ = palias/nalias, uniform or geometric ($\propto N^{2/3}$, the transit probability) weights; or one run per $N$, compared afterwards.

### Accuracy and checks

- Gladman's criterion against a numpy transcription on 200 random eccentric pairs: 2.2e-16; its circular limit is 3.4640, 3.4637, 3.4624, 3.4563, 3.4283 mutual Hill radii at $\mu$ = 1e-7 to 1e-3, tending to $2\sqrt{3}$ = 3.4641. AMD, critical AMD and $\beta$ against numpy/brentq on 100 systems of two to four planets: 1.9e-15. Two Jupiters around a Sun 3.0 $R_H$ apart are rejected and 4.0 accepted (`test/make_viability_reference.py`, `node test/viability.test.mjs`).
- With a flat likelihood the sampler's $\ln Z$ with the crossing test is −2.197 against the analytic $\ln V$ = −2.282 (expected scatter 0.15). Two planets in 30 simulated velocities (25 m/s, $e$ = 0.05 and 0.10): $\ln Z$ = −161.69 ± 0.22 without tests, −161.45 (crossing, $\ln V$ = −1.44), −162.00 (hill, −2.54), −161.99 (amd, −1.82): the data sit in the allowed region; a spacing of 8 $R_H$, which excludes the true pair (6.4 $R_H$), costs 49 in $\ln Z$ against $\ln V$ = −3.32.
- TOI-1873 d (three transits 900.191 and 900.186 d apart, TESS coverage of 16 sectors read from the owner's time series, `test/make_alias_reference.py`): allowed $N$ = 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, as in the owner's analysis, with the covered and missed transits of every $N$ up to 25 equal to EXOTIC's stored scan. A simulated planet with three transits 900 d apart (truth $N$ = 3): the categorical run gives $p(N{=}3)$ = 0.895 and $p(N{=}2)$ = 0.105 against 0.882 ± 0.028 and 0.117 ± 0.028 from one run per $N$, and its $\ln Z$ (3295.99 ± 0.18) equals the mean of theirs (3295.76 ± 0.16) (`node test/aliases.test.mjs`).

### Assumptions and limits

- Mutual inclinations are not known from transits and velocities, so Hill and AMD tests assume coplanar orbits. Neither criterion knows about resonances, which can protect crossing orbits (and the AMD test ignores the mean-motion-resonance overlap correction of later work).
- Masses from $K$ are minimum masses when the inclination is unknown. A planet without a mass counts as massless (only crossing is tested for it).
- The MEGNO screen integrates a few hundred orbits per likelihood call; it is for a final check of a narrow posterior, not for a broad search.

References: [Gladman 1993](#ref-gladman1993); [Chambers et al. 1996](#ref-chambers1996); [Laskar & Petit 2017](#ref-laskar2017); [Cincotta & Simó 2000](#ref-cincotta2000).

<a id="phasecurve"></a>

## 13. Phase curves and eclipse maps

Code: `src/core/phasecurve.js`

When a planet has the parameter $F_p/F_\star$ (`fpfs`), its own light is added to the model. The flux relative to the star alone is

$$
F(t) = S(t)\,T(t) + F_p(t)\,V(t)
$$

with $T$ the transit, $S$ optional stellar terms, $F_p$ the planet's flux and $V$ the visible fraction of the planet's disc. $F_p/F_\star$ is the dayside surface brightness relative to the star's, so the eclipse depth is $D = (F_p/F_\star)\,k^2$. The orbital phase is $\phi = \omega + \nu + 90^\circ$, zero at mid-eclipse and $180^\circ$ at mid-transit for any eccentricity.

### Harmonic phase curve

$$
F_p(\phi) = D\,\frac{(2 - C) + C\cos(\phi + \phi_h)}{2 - C + C\cos\phi_h} + D\left[h_{2c}(\cos 2\phi - 1) + h_{2s}\sin 2\phi\right]
$$

$C \in [0, 1]$ is the contrast, (maximum − minimum)/maximum of the first-order curve; $\phi_h$ is the hot-spot offset in degrees, positive east, so that the curve peaks $\phi_h$ before mid-eclipse; $h_{2c}$, $h_{2s}$ are second-harmonic amplitudes as fractions of the depth. By construction $F_p(0) = D$ and $F_p \ge 0$. The flux is floored at zero.

### Eclipse

In this mode the planet is a uniform disc and $V = 1 - A_\mathrm{lens}/(\pi k^2)$, with $A_\mathrm{lens}$ the area common to the stellar and planetary discs (closed form), when the planet is behind the star. The planet's own disc is occulted, with its true radius.

### Stellar terms

$$
S = 1 - A_\mathrm{ellip}\left(\frac{a}{r}\right)^{3}\cos 2\phi - A_\mathrm{beam}\left[\cos(\omega + \nu) + e\cos\omega\right]
$$

with the ellipsoidal and beaming amplitudes in ppm; both default to zero.

### Light-travel time

Optionally (it needs $R_\star$) the model is evaluated at the retarded time $t' = t - (R_\star/c)\,[\,r_\mathrm{tr}\sin i - Z(t)\,]$, one fixed-point step, which is zero at mid-transit and delays mid-eclipse by $(R_\star/c)(r_\mathrm{tr} + r_\mathrm{ecl})\sin i$, that is $2a/c$ for a circular orbit.

### Maps

In map mode the planet's surface brightness is $I(\theta, \lambda) = I_0\,[1 + \sum_{l,m} y_{lm} Y_{lm}(\theta, \lambda)]$ in real spherical harmonics up to degree 3, normalised as in starry [Luger et al. 2019](#ref-luger2019) with $Y_{00} = 1$, in a frame whose $z$ axis points to the star (longitude measured east from the substellar point) and whose $y$ axis is the orbit normal; rotation is synchronous. Out of eclipse the disc-integrated flux is analytic, $F_p = D_n\,[1 + \frac{2}{3}\,\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{o} + \frac{1}{4}\,\mathbf{o}^{T} Q\,\mathbf{o}]$, with $\mathbf{o}$ the direction to the observer and $\mathbf{v}$, $Q$ the degree-1 and degree-2 parts of the map; degree 3 contributes nothing out of eclipse. $D_n$ is set so that the unocculted flux at $\phi = 0$ equals $D$. During eclipse ingress and egress the flux of the visible part of the disc is obtained from ten moments $\frac{1}{\pi}\int x^a y^b z^c\,dA$, each a Green's-theorem line integral: closed form along the planet's limb and 12 Gauss-Legendre nodes along the stellar limb. A fit rejects maps whose disc-integrated flux is negative; rejecting maps with negative surface brightness is an option, off by default.

### Positive planets

Always: the planet's unocculted flux must be non-negative at every phase (so the nightside too); the smallest value over the orbit is found from 72 phases and a golden-section search. With `phase.positive_map` the surface brightness must also be non-negative everywhere on the sphere, zero prior mass otherwise. Its minimum is exact for degree 1 ($1 - |\mathbf{v}|$) and degree 2 (the minimum of $1 + \mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{b}^T Q\,\mathbf{b}$ on $|\mathbf{b}| = 1$, a trust-region problem: the multiplier is the root of a secular equation in the eigenbasis of $Q$, plus the "hard case"), and from a 5° grid and a pattern search for degree 3. In harmonic mode the option tests the degree-1 map of the first-order curve, which is stricter than physics requires: a contrast above 0.8 needs degree 2 or more, not a negative map. phaseSummary(requirePositive) gives no temperatures, albedo or hot spot for a model that is not physical, so posterior summaries can be taken over physical draws only.

### Temperatures

A brightness temperature is found by solving $\int B_\lambda(T_b)\,d\lambda = (F_p/F_\star)\int B_\lambda(T_\mathrm{eff})\,d\lambda$ over the band by bisection, the star being a blackbody at $T_\mathrm{eff}$. Day and night temperatures are those of the unocculted flux at $\phi = 0$ and $180^\circ$. Bond albedo and heat redistribution follow [Cowan & Agol 2011](#ref-cowan2011): $T_0 = T_\mathrm{eff}/\sqrt{a/R_\star}$, $A_B = 1 - \frac{1}{2}(3x + 5y)$, $\varepsilon = 8y/(3x + 5y)$ with $x = (T_d/T_0)^4$, $y = (T_n/T_0)^4$.

### Accuracy and checks

- Map basis curves to degree 3, through ingress and egress: max 4.6e-13 over 2256 values in 5 systems. ([Validation: Phase curves and eclipse mapping](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-phasecurve); `test/phasecurve.test.mjs`)
- Uniform-disc eclipse against batman 2.5.1: 4.9e-13 for circular orbits, 2.5e-7 at e = 0.93. ([Validation: Phase curves and eclipse mapping](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-phasecurve); `test/phasecurve.test.mjs`)
- Map curves against starry 1.2.0: max 5.6e-7 of the planet’s flux over 48 curves. ([Validation: Phase curves and eclipse mapping](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-phasecurve); `test/phasecurve.test.mjs`)
- Harmonic phase curve against EXOTIC: 5.0e-13 outside transit and eclipse. ([Validation: Phase curves and eclipse mapping](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-phasecurve); `test/phasecurve.test.mjs`)
- Brightness temperature against scipy quadrature and root finding: relative 1.6e-9 over 48 cases. ([Validation: Phase curves and eclipse mapping](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-phasecurve); `test/phasecurve.test.mjs`)
- The same model inside the fitting likelihood: χ² identical to the model used directly. ([Validation: Phase curves and eclipse mapping](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-phasecurve); `test/phasemodel.test.mjs`)
- Smallest brightness of 120 random maps of degree 1 to 3 (37 negative somewhere) against a 0.25° grid polished by Nelder-Mead in numpy (`test/make_mappos_reference.py`): 2.2e-16 (degree 1), 1.6e-15 (degree 2), 2.4e-12 (degree 3), none classified differently. The smallest flux over the orbit is within 5.6e-11 of the depth of 100,000 phases (`node test/phasepositive.test.mjs`).
- WASP-43 b eclipse map refitted with `positive_map` (PHASEPOS_FULL=1): degree 1 holds $y_{10}$ at the edge, 0.568 +0.005 −0.008 (stored, unconstrained: 0.703 ± 0.037, a map negative on 8.4% of the sphere), $y_{1,-1}$ is bounded at −0.03 ± 0.06 (stored: 0.11 +0.22 −0.24, its prior), and $\ln Z$ falls by 11.6 ($\ln V$ = −0.63 of prior mass removed). Degree 2 positive keeps $y_{10}$ = 0.705 ± 0.034 with $y_{20}$ = 0.17 ± 0.05, $y_{1,-1}$ = 0.00 ± 0.06, and $\ln Z$ 1.2 below the unconstrained degree-1 fit ($\ln V$ = −1.22).

### Assumptions and limits

- The examples fit Spitzer light curves that were already detrended elsewhere, jointly with that pipeline's own phase-curve model; instrument systematics are not modelled here, and those light curves are not independent of a degree-1 map.
- The north-south coefficient $y_{1,-1}$ is unconstrained in both map examples and runs into its prior unless the map is required to be positive, which bounds it (above).
- With several planets the fluxes are multiplied, which counts the star's light twice at the 1e-6 level.
- The star is a blackbody for brightness temperatures. Reflected light and thermal emission are not distinguished. A contrast above 0.8 corresponds to a degree-1 map that is negative near the antistellar point.
- EXOTIC's phase-curve model differs on purpose: its eclipse ingress is that of a body of radius $k\sqrt{F_p/F_\star}$ and starts late (up to 29% of the depth during ingress).

References: [Luger et al. 2019](#ref-luger2019); [Cowan & Agol 2011](#ref-cowan2011); [Stevenson et al. 2017](#ref-stevenson2017); [Kreidberg 2015](#ref-kreidberg2015); [Zellem et al. 2020](#ref-zellem2020).

<a id="exomoon"></a>

## 14. Exomoons

Code: `src/core/exomoon.js`

A planet has a moon when it has the parameter $R_m/R_\star$ (`rmoon`). Planet and moon orbit their common barycentre, which follows the planet's Keplerian orbit; the moon's orbit is circular. Parameters: $R_m/R_\star$; the moon's period $P_m$; its phase at the planet's mid-transit (0 = between planet and observer); the mass ratio $q = M_m/M_p$ (default 0, in which case the planet does not move about the barycentre); and one tilt angle about the transit chord (0 = coplanar and prograde). The separation follows from Kepler's law,

$$
\frac{a_m}{R_\star} = \frac{a}{R_\star}\left(\frac{P_m}{P}\right)^{2/3}\left(\frac{\mu}{1+\mu}\right)^{1/3}, \qquad \mu = \frac{M_p (1 + q)}{M_\star}
$$

and the positions are barycentre $- \frac{q}{1+q}\,\mathbf{d}$ for the planet and barycentre $+ \frac{1}{1+q}\,\mathbf{d}$ for the moon, $\mathbf{d}$ being the moon-planet vector. The blocked flux is that of the union of the two discs: the sum of the two single-disc terms of the [transit model](#transit) minus the flux behind the region common to planet, moon and star, a Green's-theorem sum over arcs of the three circles (20 Gauss-Legendre nodes per half-arc). A moon wholly behind or in front of the planet's disc adds nothing.

Stability is reported, not enforced: the Hill radius $r_H = (a/R_\star)(1 - e)(\mu/3)^{1/3}$, the limits of [Domingos et al. 2006](#ref-domingos2006) ($a_m < 0.4895\,r_H\,(1 - 1.0305e)$ prograde, $0.9309\,r_H\,(1 - 1.0764e)$ retrograde) and a Roche limit. The likelihood only requires that the two bodies do not overlap.

"Search for a moon" is a matched filter on the residuals of the planet-only fit: templates of a reference moon on a grid of period (uniform in frequency) and phase, with the planet's own depth and mid-time projected out; the statistic is the signal-to-noise ratio $\sum w r m / \sqrt{\sum w m^2}$. The false-alarm probability is the fraction of searches of white-noise realisations, drawn from the error bars, that reach the same value.

Timing and duration variations are compared with the amplitudes of [Kipping 2009](#ref-kipping2009): $\mathrm{TTV} = a_w / v_B$ and $\mathrm{TDV} = \bar{T}\,(2\pi a_w/P_m)/v_B$ with $a_w = a_m\,q/(1+q)$.

### Accuracy and checks

- Two overlapping discs on the star: max 6.5e-14 over 205 cases and 5 limb-darkening profiles. ([Validation: Exomoons](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-exomoon); `test/exomoon.test.mjs`)
- exomoon2.py, step by step with this kernel: planet + moon within 1.3e-8. ([Validation: Exomoons](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-exomoon); `test/exomoon.test.mjs`)
- Pandora, whole light curves: max difference 5.2e-6. ([Validation: Exomoons](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-exomoon); `test/exomoon.test.mjs`)
