- Timing and duration variations against Kipping’s formulas: within 2.4% and 0.5% of the amplitude. ([Validation: Exomoons](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-exomoon); `test/exomoon.test.mjs`)
- Search for an injected moon: found at S/N 26; 100 noise-only searches reach 5.0. ([Validation: Exomoons](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-exomoon); `test/exomoon.test.mjs`)
- Moonless light curves: 1 of 40 above the 95% level of noise (2 expected). ([Validation: Exomoons](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-exomoon); `test/exomoon.test.mjs`)

### Assumptions and limits

- The moon's orbit is circular; the star's tide on the moon is ignored (two bodies about a Keplerian barycentre); one orientation angle only. The moon's own light is not modelled.
- No real detection has been reproduced: there is none. The example is simulated.
- The configuration of the reference script this was ported from is unbound (2.4 Hill radii), which the page flags.
- The search's false-alarm rate assumes white noise with the stated error bars. The moon is not drawn in the three-dimensional view.

References: [Kipping 2009](#ref-kipping2009); [Domingos et al. 2006](#ref-domingos2006); [Heller 2014](#ref-heller2014); [Hippke & Heller 2022](#ref-hippke2022).

<a id="nbody"></a>

## 15. N-body dynamics

Code: `src/core/nbody.js`, `src/core/model.js`

With the N-body option, mid-transit times and stellar velocities come from an integration of the star and planets instead of independent Keplerian orbits. The planets' $P$, $T_0$, $e$, $\omega$, $i$ (and an optional node angle) are read as osculating elements at a stated epoch, in Jacobi coordinates with planets ordered by period, in the frame of the [conventions](#conventions). Units are au, days and solar masses. With all planet masses zero the result is the Keplerian model.

- **Wisdom-Holman map** (default): the splitting of [Wisdom & Holman 1991](#ref-wisdom1991) in Jacobi coordinates as in WHFast [Rein & Tamayo 2015](#ref-rein2015whfast), drift-kick-drift, with the Kepler drift solved in universal variables and symplectic correctors [Wisdom 2006](#ref-wisdom2006) of order 5 by default. The step is fixed at $\min_p [P_p (1 - e_p)^{3/2}/\sqrt{1 + e_p}]$ divided by 30 (20 in the example and the companion search).
- **IAS15**: the 15th-order Gauss-Radau integrator of [Rein & Spiegel 2015](#ref-rein2015ias15) (after [Everhart 1985](#ref-everhart1985)) with adaptive steps, precision parameter $10^{-9}$. It is used only when selected; a close encounter under the Wisdom-Holman map (separation below one mutual Hill radius) is reported with advice to rerun, not handled automatically.
- **Transit times**: the root of the star-centred sky-plane condition, by default the conjunction $X\cos\Omega + Y\sin\Omega = 0$ in the likelihood (or the minimum separation $\mathbf{R}_\mathrm{sky}\cdot\mathbf{V}_\mathrm{sky} = 0$ as in TTVFast [Deck et al. 2014](#ref-deck2014)), with the planet in front; refined by Newton iteration on a two-body arc.
- **Velocity**: $-\dot{Z}_\star$ of the star in the barycentric frame, positive when receding.
- **In the likelihood**: observed mid-transit times are matched to the nearest simulated transit. With `nbody.linear` a weighted straight line in epoch is fitted to each planet's residuals inside the likelihood, so the transiting planet's own $T_0$ and $P$ need not be sampled.

Stability is reported from the mutual Hill separation (two planets are Hill-stable beyond $2\sqrt{3}$ mutual Hill radii, [Gladman 1993](#ref-gladman1993); with three or more planets a separation below 10 is flagged, [Chambers et al. 1996](#ref-chambers1996)), orbit crossing, the AMD criterion of [Laskar & Petit 2017](#ref-laskar2017) and, on request, a short integration with a shadow particle. "Search for an unseen companion" scores a grid of perturber mass and period (eight starting phases each) by the $\chi^2$ of the observed times against the integration with a straight line profiled out, then polishes the best cell by Nelder-Mead. The analytic amplitudes of [Lithwick, Xie & Wu 2012](#ref-lithwick2012) and [Agol et al. 2005](#ref-agol2005) are available for comparison.

### Accuracy and checks

- Transit times against REBOUND 5.2.2 (IAS15), EXOTIC’s example system: 1.3e-6 s over 610 transits. ([Validation: N-body dynamics](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-nbody); `test/nbody.test.mjs`)
- Same map as REBOUND’s WHFast: positions within 2.0e-12 AU after 8000 steps. ([Validation: N-body dynamics](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-nbody); `test/nbody.test.mjs`)
- One planet: identical to the Keplerian model: timing 3.4e-6 s over 400 orbits, velocity 1.6e-9 m/s. ([Validation: N-body dynamics](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-nbody); `test/nbody.test.mjs`)
- Critical angular-momentum deficit against a brute-force minimum: relative 3.8e-12 over 25 cases. ([Validation: N-body dynamics](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-nbody); `test/nbody.test.mjs`)
- Unseen companion recovered from 72 transit times: 0.1040 M Jup (injected 0.1), mean period 5.3336 d (5.3322). ([Validation: N-body dynamics](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-nbody); `test/nbody.test.mjs`)
- The same dynamics inside the fitting likelihood: χ² 82.9 against 82.9 from the other integrator directly. ([Validation: N-body dynamics](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-nbody); `test/nbodymodel.test.mjs`)

### Assumptions and limits

- Light curves and mid-eclipse times from the integration are described in the next section (Photodynamics). Light-travel time is optional (`nbody.ltt`).
- A fit that samples the transiting planet's own period and $T_0$ as osculating elements did not converge in 150,000 likelihood calls, which is why the straight line is profiled by default; mean-ephemeris elements (next section) make that fit converge at about six integrations per call. A profiled parameter is not marginalised: the evidence of such a fit is not comparable with that of a Keplerian fit, and the uncertainties are conditional on the best line.
- The $\chi^2$ surface of a perturber has period aliases every few thousandths of a day. The search returns one solution that fits, not the only one.
- TTVFast, given the same Jacobi elements, differs by hundreds of seconds because it defines them differently (stored test output); compare codes through state vectors or transit times, not elements.

References: [Wisdom & Holman 1991](#ref-wisdom1991); [Wisdom 2006](#ref-wisdom2006); [Rein & Tamayo 2015](#ref-rein2015whfast); [Rein & Spiegel 2015](#ref-rein2015ias15); [Everhart 1985](#ref-everhart1985); [Rein & Liu 2012](#ref-rein2012); [Deck et al. 2014](#ref-deck2014); [Lithwick, Xie & Wu 2012](#ref-lithwick2012); [Agol et al. 2005](#ref-agol2005); [Holman & Murray 2005](#ref-holman2005); [Gladman 1993](#ref-gladman1993); [Chambers et al. 1996](#ref-chambers1996); [Laskar & Petit 2017](#ref-laskar2017); [Pearson 2019](#ref-pearson2019).

<a id="photodynamics"></a>

## 16. Photodynamics

Code: `src/core/nbody.js (dynamicalModel, simulate, osculatingFromMean, megno)`, `src/core/model.js (spec.nbody)`

With `spec.nbody` set and a light curve in the fit, the light curve is computed from the same integration as the transit times and velocities. The integrator writes every body's position and velocity at evenly spaced nodes (150 per orbit of the innermost planet by default) only over the spans covered by data; each planet's sky-plane position relative to the star at a sample time is interpolated by cubic Hermite polynomials from the positions and velocities at the neighbouring nodes, and the separation is passed to the transit kernel of the transit-model section, through the same exposure averaging as Keplerian curves.

**Light-travel time** (`nbody.ltt`): each body is taken at its retarded time, with the barycentre's sky plane as reference, so a transit is seen about $a/c$ early and an eclipse about $a/c$ late.

**Mid-eclipse times** in the timing likelihood come from the same integration (roots of the superior-conjunction condition).

**Mean-ephemeris elements** (`nbody.elements: "mean"`): a planet's sampled period and $T_0$ are those of the straight line through its simulated transits over the span of the data; the osculating elements at the reference epoch are found by fixed-point iteration (each step one integration). This removes the ridge between a companion's mass and the transiting planet's osculating period that defeats sampling in osculating elements.

**MEGNO** [Cincotta & Simó 2000](#ref-cincotta2000) is integrated alongside a short run (variational equations, Gauss–Radau quadrature on the IAS15 nodes): about 2 for a regular orbit, growing linearly for a chaotic one; it enters the stability findings.

### Accuracy and checks

- `node test/nbodyphoto.test.mjs` (references from REBOUND 5.2.2 and batman, `test/make_nbodyphoto_reference.py`): with all masses zero the photodynamical curve equals the Keplerian one to 1.0e-9 of the flux (3.6e-14 at 600 nodes per orbit); a strongly perturbed pair (1 and 2 $M_\mathrm{J}$ at 10 and 20.3 d, 2819 points over 125 d, where the Keplerian curve is wrong by 12,049 ppm) agrees with REBOUND IAS15 positions through batman's kernel to 0.008 ppm with IAS15, 57 ppm with the Wisdom–Holman map at its defaults and 14 ppm at 60 steps per orbit; 30-minute exposures 0.004 ppm; light-travel time 0.02 ppm against REBOUND at retarded times. Mid-eclipse times: 3.8e-8 s from REBOUND for 18 eclipses. MEGNO 2.0004, 1.9955, 1.9987 on the example system after 2000 orbits (REBOUND 2.0008, 2.0020).
- Mean elements: periods recovered to 1.6e-11 d after a round trip; a five-parameter fit of the timing example (both planets' ephemerides and the companion's mass) converged in 19,032 calls, companion $0.1004 \pm 0.0063\,M_\mathrm{J}$ (injected 0.100), with `NBODY_FIT=1`.

### Assumptions and limits

- Planets are treated one at a time in the light curve: the area two planets share on the disc during a mutual event is counted twice. A planet with its own light or a moon keeps a Keplerian curve.
- The Wisdom–Holman map's timing error grows with time and with the square of the masses (7 s over 125 d for the pair above); pairs of giant planets with precise photometry need IAS15 or more steps per orbit.
- The straight-line profile (`nbody.linear`) corrects times only and is refused together with a light curve. Mean elements cost about six integrations per call and are not found inside a mean-motion resonance (the point is rejected).
- The value of MEGNO for a chaotic orbit is not reproducible between codes, only "about 2" against "much more"; the Lyapunov time from a run stopped at MEGNO = 20 is an order of magnitude.

References: [Rein & Spiegel 2015](#ref-rein2015ias15); [Rein & Tamayo 2015](#ref-rein2015whfast); [Wisdom & Holman 1991](#ref-wisdom1991); [Cincotta & Simó 2000](#ref-cincotta2000); [Kreidberg 2015](#ref-kreidberg2015).

<a id="spectroscopy"></a>

## 17. Time-series spectroscopy

Code: `src/core/spectroscopy.js`, `src/core/missionbands.js`, `src/core/model.js (data.regressors)`, `src/spectra/`

Input is extracted one-dimensional spectra over time: JWST `x1dints.fits` files (both pipeline layouts, one row per integration or one extension per integration, segments joined in time and detectors in wavelength) or a table of flux against time and wavelength (CSV, ECSV). There is no spectral extraction from images.

### Cleaning and binning

A point more than 5 robust standard deviations from an 11-point running median in time is replaced. A column is dropped when more than 20% of its points are bad, when its median flux is not positive or differs by more than 50% from its neighbours', or when its error bars are five times the typical ones. Channels are sums over columns (constant resolving power, constant width, $N$ channels, or a fixed number of columns), with errors added in quadrature, normalised by their median. Error bars are widened to the point-to-point scatter when that is larger (the default; pipeline errors or scatter alone can be chosen).

### Baseline

Every light curve, white or spectroscopic, goes through the one likelihood (`buildProblem`) with optional regressors $x_k$ per epoch (scaled time, its square, step functions at given times):

$$
F(t) = m(t)\,e^{a_2 X(t)}\left(a_1 + \sum_k c_k\,x_k(t)\right)
$$

with $a_1$ and the $c_k$ integrated out analytically together (a Gaussian integral with the determinant of the weighted normal matrix), each $c_k$ under a flat prior of width 2.

### White light, then channels

The white light curve is fitted by nested sampling for $k$, $T_0$ and $i$; $a/R_\star$ is fixed or follows from Kepler's law with $R_\star$ free under a normal prior. Each channel is then fitted for its depth ($k$, or $F_p/F_\star$ for an eclipse) with the geometry fixed at the white-light solution and limb-darkening coefficients from the PHOENIX table [Husser et al. 2013](#ref-husser2013) for the channel's wavelength range and the star. With one free parameter the posterior is integrated on a 241-point grid of the same likelihood. Limb darkening with a normal prior, or the geometry with normal priors, sends the channel fit to the nested sampler instead.

### Products

The spectrum with 16th–84th percentile errors; per-channel residual rms against the error bars; the binned-rms test of the noise section; the depth in atmospheric scale heights $H = k_B T_\mathrm{eq}/(\mu m_\mathrm{H} g)$ for interpretation (with $\mu$ chosen by the user, 2.3 by default), the change of depth per scale height being $2 k H/R_\star$.

### Simulator

Simulated observations use photon noise from a black-body star seen through a telescope of collecting area $A$ (Ariel 0.63 m² [Tinetti et al. 2018](#ref-tinetti2018), JWST 25.4 m²) and a throughput $\tau$, plus a noise floor $f$ (for Ariel the throughput is each channel's published efficiency, the photon variance carries a 40% margin and 40 ppm$\sqrt{\mathrm{hr}}$ of gain noise is added, after ArielRad; see the Atmosphere section, Retrieval):

$$
N_e = A\,\tau\,\Delta t\,\pi\left(\frac{R_\star}{d}\right)^2 \int \frac{2c}{\lambda^4}\frac{\mathrm{d}\lambda}{e^{hc/\lambda k_B T} - 1}, \qquad \sigma^2 = \frac{(1+x)^2}{N_e} + f^2\,\frac{T_{14}}{\Delta t}
$$

$\tau$ (0.3) and $f$ (20 ppm Ariel, 10 ppm JWST) are editable inputs and are not taken from mission documents. This is a simple radiometric estimate, not ArielRad or PandExo.

### Accuracy and checks

- `node test/spectroscopy.test.mjs` (44 checks): readers against astropy, exact (real G395H files to 2.4e-15); the marginal likelihood with regressors against a `scipy.integrate.tplquad` integral to 9.4e-5 in $\ln L$, coefficients against `numpy.linalg.solve` to 1.4e-9; photon rate against `scipy.integrate.quad` to 8.4e-9; Ariel-to-JWST noise ratio 6.300 $= \sqrt{25.4/0.64}$.
- Injection and recovery: pulls (recovered − injected)/$\sigma$ of mean 0.084 and standard deviation 0.980 over 228 simulated Ariel channels (70% within 1$\sigma$, 96% within 2$\sigma$); 0.296 and 0.981 over 36 channels made with batman [Kreidberg 2015](#ref-kreidberg2015) with the geometry at the truth, 0.471 and 0.978 with the geometry from the white-light fit.
- Real data, WASP-39 b with NIRSpec G395H (JWST ERS program 1366, standard-pipeline `x1dints`): the mirror-tilt step is found automatically (−3275 ppm, 75$\sigma$); white-light depth 21324 ± 13 ppm, residual rms 136 ppm. At $R = 100$ (56 channels) the spectrum follows the published one [Alderson et al. 2023](#ref-alderson2023) with correlation 0.974 and a scatter of the differences of 91 ppm (1.10 combined $\sigma$), but lies **202 ppm lower on average**. The offset is not explained (geometry, fixed limb darkening and the standard-pipeline extraction against the paper's custom reductions are candidates; none was isolated). This test needs 207 MB of public files and is skipped without them.

### Assumptions and limits

- Channel error bars do not include the uncertainty of the shared geometry; a change of the white-light inclination moves all channels together.
- All bands are top-hats; no measured throughput curves are used. The JWST and Ariel wavelength limits are those of the mission documentation and should be checked against the instrument's current values before quoting.
- Limb darkening beyond 5.5 µm (MIRI LRS, the red end of Ariel AIRS-Ch1) lies outside the PHOENIX table and is extrapolated; the page flags it.
- Not read: HST/WFC3 spatial scans and any two-dimensional product (`calints`, `rateints`). NIRSpec PRISM data and the published PRISM spectrum were not compared. Sessions hold the binned channel light curves, not the cube.
- Exposure averaging uses midpoint sub-samples; batman's end-to-end spacing differs by 3.7 ppm in the test.

References: [Alderson et al. 2023](#ref-alderson2023); [Tinetti et al. 2018](#ref-tinetti2018); [Husser et al. 2013](#ref-husser2013); [Kreidberg 2015](#ref-kreidberg2015); [Winn et al. 2008](#ref-winn2008); [Mancini et al. 2018](#ref-mancini2018).

<a id="atmosphere"></a>

## 18. Atmospheres: structure, chemistry, spectra, escape

Code: `src/core/atmosphere.js`, `src/core/opacity.js`, `src/core/continuum.js`, `src/core/transmission.js`, `src/core/emission.js`, `src/core/rtmodel.js`, `src/core/chemistry.js`, `src/core/escape.js`, `src/core/ionization.js`, `src/core/colour.js`, `src/viz/atmoview.js`, `src/atmosphere/`

A planet, a temperature profile and a composition are turned into a transmission spectrum, an emission spectrum, and a picture. The model is one-dimensional: one column of gas stands for the whole planet. Everything on the Atmosphere page comes from the single function `forwardModel`.

### Structure

Layers are uniform in $\ln P$ (60 or 80 between the top, $10^{-8}$ bar on the page, and 100 bar), each at one temperature. With gravity $g = GM/r^2$ and an ideal gas, hydrostatic balance integrates exactly over a layer of constant $T$ and mean molecular weight $\mu$:

$$
\frac{1}{r_{k+1}} - \frac{1}{r_k} = \frac{k_B T}{\mu m_u G M}\,\ln\frac{P_{k+1}}{P_k}
$$

The radius given for the planet is placed at a reference pressure (10 mbar by default). Temperature profiles: isothermal; the irradiated grey solution of [Guillot 2010](#ref-guillot2010) (its eq. 29, with the planet-wide average $f = 1/4$); the three-layer profile of [Madhusudhan & Seager 2009](#ref-madhusudhan2009).

### A profile that follows from the gas

The fourth choice of profile is worked out from the atmosphere itself (`src/core/climate.js`). It keeps the form of the grey solution, $T^4 = \frac{3}{4}T_\mathrm{int}^4(\frac{2}{3} + \tau) + \frac{3}{4}T_\mathrm{irr}^4 f\,[\frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{\gamma\sqrt3} + (\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt3} - \frac{1}{\gamma\sqrt3})e^{-\sqrt3\tau_v}]$ with $\gamma = \tau_v/\tau$, but takes its two optical depths from the real, non-grey gas at every level: $\tau_v = -\mu_0 \ln$ of the share of the star's light (a blackbody of its temperature) that reaches the level through the model's absorption, wavelength by wavelength and quadrature point by quadrature point, and $\tau = -\bar\mu \ln$ of the share of the level's own blackbody radiation that escapes to space ($\mu_0 = 0.5$, $\bar\mu = 1/1.66$; scattering holds heat in and absorbs no starlight). Mean opacities do not serve: from these tables a Rosseland mean is set by the floor of the windows between bands and a Planck mean by saturated line cores, each wrong by orders of magnitude.

The atmosphere is rebuilt on each new set of temperatures, so chemistry, condensation, ionization and opacity follow them, and the passes continue until no layer moves by more than 2 K. One number $c$ multiplies $T^4$ and is adjusted until the model's own emission spectrum, integrated over wavelength, equals the flux the planet must lose, $\sigma(4fT_\mathrm{eq}^4 + T_\mathrm{int}^4)$; $c$ near 1 means the closure needed no help ($f = 1/4$ for the whole planet, $1/2$ for a day side that keeps its heat). Layers steeper than an adiabat ($d\ln T/d\ln P > 2/7$) are put on it. Above $10^{-5}$ bar, where the opacity tables end, the profile is held at its value there: in gas that thin the strong lines of sodium and potassium scatter starlight instead of turning it into heat, and counted as absorbers they would heat the top by hundreds of kelvin and dissociate its hydrogen. The model has no thermosphere. Clouds enter: a deck as an opaque floor, particles through their absorption and scattering, partial cover as the mix of two columns. The planet's energy budget is therefore met with the real spectrum, but each layer's is not: this is not radiative-convective equilibrium.

Where the gas absorbs starlight better than it holds heat, $\gamma > 1$, the temperature rises with height. With gas-phase TiO and VO the day side of WASP-121 b comes out inverted by about 250 K between 20 and 2 mbar, as a retrieval of its eclipse spectrum finds [Mikal-Evans et al. 2019](#ref-mikalevans2019); without those two gases, or once they have rained out, it does not.

### Condensation and rain-out

A gas cannot exceed what its condensate allows (`src/core/condensation.js`). For water, ammonia and methane that is the saturation vapour pressure, $x \le h\,p_\mathrm{sat}(T)/P$ with $h$ the saturation allowed (fits of Buck for water, of Ackerman & Marley 2001 for ammonia ice, the NIST Antoine fit and [Fray & Schmitt 2009](#ref-frayschmitt2009) for liquid and solid methane). For solids made from several gases the published condensation curves $10^4/T = a - b\log P - c\,[\mathrm{M/H}]$ [Morley et al. 2012](#ref-morley2012); [Visscher et al. 2010](#ref-visscher2010); [Wakeford et al. 2017](#ref-wakeford2017) are read the other way: at $(T, P)$ the gas holds the fraction $10^{[\mathrm{M/H}]_\mathrm{sat} - [\mathrm{M/H}]}$ of the limiting element, $[\mathrm{M/H}]_\mathrm{sat} = (a - b\log P - 10^4/T)/c$, or all of it. Perovskite removes TiO and VO, Na$_2$S sodium, KCl potassium; iron, the silicates, corundum and the other sulfides mark where a cloud begins.

With rain-out, above the level where a gas first condenses it keeps no more than the least it was allowed on the way up, even where the air is warmer again: the cold trap. That is what leaves Titan's stratosphere with less methane than its surface, Jupiter's upper troposphere without water, and a hot Jupiter cooler than about 2000 K at depth without TiO. The chemistry is not solved again without the condensed elements, and nothing lifts material back up. A particle layer can be placed at a condensate's base; its optical depth and grain size remain inputs.

### Hazes of a real material, and other bulk gases

A particle layer may be given a material in place of the analytic efficiency: Mie theory for homogeneous spheres (`src/core/mie.js`, the algorithm of Bohren & Huffman) with measured optical constants, averaged over a log-normal spread of radii, gives the extinction and the single-scattering albedo at every wavelength. The material shipped is the tholin of [Khare et al. 1984](#ref-khare1984), a laboratory analogue of Titan's haze. The layer's optical depth can be spread as $\tau(<P) \propto P^x$; $x < 1$ puts relatively more haze high up. The gas that fills the atmosphere can be nitrogen or carbon dioxide instead of hydrogen and helium, with collision-induced absorption of N$_2$-N$_2$, N$_2$-CH$_4$ and N$_2$-H$_2$ from HITRAN, each band interpolated within the temperatures it was measured or computed at.

Titan and Jupiter are preset worlds (`src/core/worlds.js`) that test these parts against measurements: the altitudes of Huygens's profile [Fulchignoni et al. 2005](#ref-fulchignoni2005), methane at the surface and above the cold trap [Niemann et al. 2010](#ref-niemann2010), the altitude and colour slope of the haze in Cassini's solar occultations [Robinson et al. 2014](#ref-robinson2014) (to which the haze's three numbers are tuned), and Jupiter's cloud bases against an equilibrium cloud model [Atreya & Wong 2005](#ref-atreya2005); condensation temperatures are checked against [Lodders 2003](#ref-lodders2003).

### The star

Eclipse depths divide the planet's flux by the star's. The star is a model atmosphere where one is available (`src/core/stellarspec.js`): the PHOENIX-ACES specific intensities that the limb darkening table is built from [Husser et al. 2013](#ref-husser2013), integrated over the disc, $F_\lambda = 2\pi\int_0^1 I_\lambda(\mu)\,\mu\,d\mu$, on 420 bins from 0.1 to 5.5 µm for 519 models (2300-8000 K, $\log g$ 4-5.5, [Fe/H] $-0.5$ to $+0.5$), interpolated linearly in the three parameters on $\log F$. Beyond 5.5 µm a blackbody of the star's temperature is joined on, scaled to the model near 4 µm. A K or M dwarf is brighter than its blackbody near 1.6 µm and fainter beyond 4 µm, so eclipse depths over a blackbody star are off by 10 to 20%. Beyond the models the tail falls as $(\lambda/4\,\mu\mathrm{m})^{-0.08}$, as a photosphere's brightness temperature does.

**The star from its magnitudes** (the Star page, `src/core/sed.js`). A star of angular diameter $\theta$ sends the fraction $(\theta/2)^2$ of its surface flux to the observer, dimmed by $10^{-0.4 A_V k(\lambda)}$ with the extinction curve of Fitzpatrick (1999) at $R_V = 3.1$. Each catalogue magnitude is computed through its own passband, counting photons or energy as its detector does, with passbands and zero points from the SVO Filter Profile Service. The nested sampler finds $T_\mathrm{eff}$, $\log g$, [Fe/H], $\theta$, $A_V$ and one scatter term added to every error bar; a parallax then gives $R_\star = \theta d/2$ and $L = 4\pi d^2 F_\mathrm{bol}$. Against interferometric diameters three of four benchmark stars agree within 2% and 40 K (with no extinction, as befits stars within 50 pc); the fourth, HD 189733, comes out 7% smaller and 152 K hotter, as it does in the published fit of AstroARIADNE. The page shows the posterior as a corner plot, the sampler's evidence and diagnostics, a comparison of fits by $\Delta\ln Z$ and LaTeX tables; magnitudes and the parallax can be looked up in Gaia DR3, 2MASS, AllWISE and Tycho-2 through VizieR. A low-resolution spectrum can be matched against the same grid (`src/core/specmatch.js`), with a smooth polynomial factor for an uncalibrated slope; the models' 5 nm sampling rules out line-by-line matching of echelle spectra. Magnitudes hardly constrain gravity or metallicity, and the grid holds main-sequence stars from 2300 to 8000 K only.

### Retrieval

A retrieval (`src/core/retrieval.js`) frees chosen quantities of the model (the profile's numbers, [M/H], C/O or single abundances, the radius at the reference pressure, haze and cloud, the night-side contrast), each with a prior of the same kinds as the light-curve fits, and samples a Gaussian likelihood over any number of spectra with the nested sampler: transit depths against the limb column, eclipse depths against the day side, and the night side's flux ratio where a phase curve gives it. Two descriptions of the same data are compared by $\Delta\ln Z$. The model is averaged over each data bin, its own bins weighted by how much of each lies inside. On the Retrieval page, and wherever a fit is asked for without other settings, priors are uniform between stated limits, the model has 30 layers, and the opacity bins are joined as far as leaves three to a data bin; the shaded band on the page's spectrum is the 16 to 84% range of the model over 60 draws of the posterior. Simulated Ariel observations take their noise from the recipe ArielRad publishes (photon noise with a 40% margin on its variance, 40 ppm$\sqrt{\mathrm{hr}}$ of gain noise, a 20 ppm floor) and agree with its photon noise for HD 209458 to 8%. This likelihood is not yet part of the one the light curves use.

### Speed

Three quarters of a run is the mixing of the gases' k-distributions. For many runs on one data set the tables can be cut to its wavelength range and neighbouring bins joined (`prepareTables`), the mixing loop runs in WebAssembly where available (the same arithmetic, 2.6 times faster), and results are kept while their inputs stay the same. A model over 0.6 to 5.3 µm at resolving power 100 with 40 layers takes 26 ms where the full tables take 274 ms, within 3.5 ppm rms.

### Composition and chemical equilibrium

Mixing ratios are either typed, constant with height, with H$_2$ and He filling the rest, or taken from chemical equilibrium. For equilibrium the page interpolates a table computed with FastChem [Stock et al. 2018](#ref-stock2018) on 40 temperatures (300-4000 K), 21 pressures ($10^{-8}$-100 bar), 11 metallicities ([M/H] from $-1$ to $2.5$) and 14 values of C/O (0.1-1.5), on the logarithm of each mixing ratio: linearly in $\ln T$ and $\log P$, and by a monotone cubic through the nodes in [M/H] and C/O, so that a spectrum has no kink in either at the table's nodes. Metallicity scales every element heavier than helium from the solar values of [Asplund et al. 2021](#ref-asplund2021); C/O is then set by changing oxygen. The star's own [Fe/H], when the catalogue has it, is shown beside the metallicity control as the natural starting point.

The table is gas phase only: nothing condenses or rains out in it (condensation is applied afterwards, when switched on; see below). TiO, VO, Na and K are therefore overstated at temperatures where they would be locked in solids (below roughly 1500-2000 K and 1000 K), and water forms no cloud. A quench pressure freezes the carriers of carbon, oxygen and nitrogen (CH$_4$, CO, CO$_2$, H$_2$O, NH$_3$, HCN, N$_2$) at lower pressures to their values there, the usual one-parameter stand-in for vertical mixing; no kinetics is computed.

### Opacity

Line opacity is correlated-k: tables of twelve gases from ExoMolOP [Chubb et al. 2021](#ref-chubb2021) reduced to resolving power 200 and 12 quadrature points, interpolated bilinearly in $\ln P$ and $1/T$ on $\log\sigma$, and combined species by species under random overlap, each combined distribution put back on the quadrature points as the mean of $\ln k$ over each point's interval. Continuum: collision-induced absorption of H$_2$-H$_2$ and H$_2$-He [Karman et al. 2019](#ref-karman2019); Rayleigh scattering of H$_2$, He and seven other gases; H$^-$ when the chemistry supplies it. Aerosols, each with its own parameters: an opaque grey deck; a power law $\sigma \propto \lambda^{s}$; the gas's Rayleigh scattering multiplied by a factor; a layer of grains of one radius $a$ with the extinction efficiency of [Kitzmann & Heng 2018](#ref-kitzmann2018),

The source tables were checked against a conservation rule: a line's cross-section integrated over frequency is $(\pi e^2/m_e c)\,f$ at every pressure. The ten molecules keep their integrated strength to a few per cent between $10^{-5}$ and 10 bar. Sodium and potassium do not: the cores of their D lines are right at 10 bar and too strong as $1/P$ below it ($1.7\times10^5$ times at $10^{-5}$ bar). Those bins are recomputed when the tables are built, as Voigt profiles with the NIST oscillator strengths that meet the source's own far wings; the shipped tables then agree with the recomputed full-resolution ones to 2 ppm rms in transit depth.

$$
Q_\mathrm{ext} = \frac{5}{Q_0\,x^{-4} + x^{0.2}}, \qquad x = \frac{2\pi a}{\lambda}
$$

and a covered fraction $f$ of the planet, the spectrum being $f$ times the cloudy column plus $1-f$ times the clear one [Line & Parmentier 2016](#ref-line2016).

### Transmission

One ray per level crosses the spherical shells; inside each shell the pressure along the ray is integrated by four-point Gauss-Legendre quadrature. With $\tau_\lambda(b)$ the optical depth of the ray of impact parameter $b$, the transit depth is

$$
\delta_\lambda = \frac{1}{R_\star^2}\left[R_\mathrm{base}^2 + 2\int_{R_\mathrm{base}}^{R_\mathrm{top}} \left(1 - \langle e^{-\tau_\lambda(b)}\rangle_g\right) b\,db\right]
$$

by the trapezoid rule in $b^2$, the transmittance (not the optical depth) averaged over the quadrature points $g$ of each bin. Under an opaque deck every ray below its top is blocked, and a level is moved onto the deck so that it does not snap to the grid. No refraction, no scattering into the beam.

### Emission

The formal solution through isothermal layers at eight Gauss angles, plane-parallel, absorption only: $F_\lambda = 2\pi\int_0^1 I_\lambda(\mu)\,\mu\,d\mu$ with $I_\lambda(\mu) = \sum_k B_\lambda(T_k)\,(e^{-\tau_{k}/\mu} - e^{-\tau_{k+1}/\mu})$. Scattering removes light from the transit beam but is not a thermal source, so it enters the transmission spectrum only. The eclipse depth is $(R_p/R_\star)^2 F_p/F_\star$ over a blackbody star.

### A cooler night side

With a night side cooler by $\Delta T$ the same one-dimensional model is run for three columns (`dayNightModel`): the day side with the profile as given, which supplies the emission spectrum (an eclipse shows the day side); the night side with the profile's irradiation temperature lowered by $\Delta T$; and the limb, each layer at the mean of the two, which supplies the transmission spectrum. Chemistry, ionization and opacity follow each column's own temperatures. The cutaway draws the day column toward the star and the night column away from it, blended by $(1 + \cos\phi)/2$ in between; the 3D view blends the interior's glow the same way. This is an interpolation between two profiles, not a circulation model.

### Ionization by starlight

Chemistry puts atoms in the gas; starlight ionizes them high up. In each layer, in steady state, for hydrogen, sodium and potassium,

$$
n_0\,(J + q\,n_e) = (\alpha_r + \alpha_3)\,n_e\,n_+, \qquad J = \int F_\lambda\,\sigma_\lambda\,e^{-\sigma_\lambda N/\mu_0}\,d\lambda
$$

with the photoionization cross-sections of [Verner et al. 1996](#ref-verner1996), radiative recombination of [Verner & Ferland 1996](#ref-vernerferland1996), electron-impact ionization of [Voronov 1997](#ref-voronov1997) and a three-body term, following [Pearson 2019](#ref-pearson2019). $N$ is the column of the neutral atom above, found by solving the layers from the top down; $\mu_0 = 0.5$ is the day-side mean slant. Hydrogen (present as atoms when the composition comes from chemical equilibrium) is ionized by the star's extreme ultraviolet, taken from the Sun's history at the star's age [Ribas et al. 2005](#ref-ribas2005), scaled to the orbit and spread evenly from 10 to 91.2 nm, and is shielded by the H and H$_2$ above. Sodium and potassium are ionized by the near ultraviolet of a blackbody at the star's temperature. Potassium's cross-section is the 4s-shell fit of Verner & Yakovlev (1995, A&AS 109, 125); no fits for its recombination or electron-impact rates are carried, so it recombines at sodium's rate (for both alkalis recombination to the ground state, which detailed balance gives from the cross-section, is under 0.1% of the total) and its electron-impact rate is sodium's fit at potassium's ionization energy. The electrons of all three, and any from the chemistry, enter each other's recombination. The neutral parts replace the mixing ratios, so sodium's opacity falls where it is ionized: at the pressures of its line cores, well above where the continuum forms. The chemistry carries no other free atoms, and molecules are not photodissociated.

### Escape (in the code, not on the page)

`src/core/escape.js` holds estimates of size, not a hydrodynamic calculation; they were taken off the page because the model's spectra hardly respond to them and nothing there can yet be tested against data. The energy-limited mass-loss rate [Watson et al. 1981](#ref-watson1981); [Erkaev et al. 2007](#ref-erkaev2007) is

$$
\dot M = \frac{\eta\,\pi F_\mathrm{XUV}\,R_p R_\mathrm{XUV}^2}{G M_p K}, \qquad K = 1 - \frac{3}{2\xi} + \frac{1}{2\xi^3}, \quad \xi = \frac{a}{R_p}\left(\frac{M_p}{3M_\star}\right)^{1/3}
$$

with heating efficiency $\eta$ (0.2), $R_\mathrm{XUV}$ the radius where a column of atomic hydrogen reaches optical depth one for $\sigma = 5\times10^{-18}$ cm$^2$ in an isothermal atmosphere, and $F_\mathrm{XUV}$ from the Sun's history, $29.7\,t_\mathrm{Gyr}^{-1.23}$ erg cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ at 1 AU [Ribas et al. 2005](#ref-ribas2005), held constant before 0.1 Gyr and scaled to the orbit. A hydrogen wind of flux $F_\mathrm{H}$ carries along species lighter than the crossover mass [Hunten et al. 1987](#ref-hunten1987); [Zahnle & Kasting 1986](#ref-zahnle1986),

$$
m_c = m_\mathrm{H} + \frac{k_B T\,F_\mathrm{H}}{b\,g\,X_\mathrm{H}}, \qquad x_i = \frac{m_c - m_i}{m_c - m_\mathrm{H}} \;(m_i < m_c),\ \text{else } 0
$$

where $b$ is the binary diffusion coefficient times number density (measured power laws for H with He, D and O; for C, N, S and Na the H-O value scaled by reduced mass) and $x_i$ the fractionation factor. If a share $f$ of the hydrogen remains, a species' abundance relative to hydrogen has grown by $f^{\,x_i - 1}$ (Rayleigh distillation). `escapeHistory` integrates $\dot M$ and the $x_i$ over the star's age in 200 steps of log time for a gas envelope of a stated share of the planet's mass.

### The picture

The 3D view follows one ray per pixel through the same layers: starlight scattered once toward the viewer, attenuated on the way in and out, absent in the planet's shadow; behind the limb the limb-darkened star seen through the atmosphere; below, the interior's own emission and a reflectance from a two-stream estimate. The extinction of each layer in each colour channel is obtained from the model's limb transmittance by onion peeling, so the ring drawn in transit is the spectrum's. Colour is true colour: the spectrum from 0.38 to 0.75 µm under the star's light through the CIE 1931 colour-matching functions (the analytic fits of Wyman, Sloan & Shirley 2013) to sRGB.

### Accuracy and checks

- Eight molecules mixed, same k-tables and interpolation as petitRADTRANS 3.4.0: transit 3.4 ppm rms, 13.8 ppm at worst; flux 0.36% rms. ([Validation: Atmosphere: transmission and emission spectra](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-atmosphere); `test/rt_reference.test.mjs`)
- H2O, CO, Na, K, TiO and VO on an ultra-hot Jupiter, from 0.35 µm: transit 1.2 ppm rms; flux 0.41% rms. ([Validation: Atmosphere: transmission and emission spectra](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-atmosphere); `test/rt_reference.test.mjs`)
- Each of the twelve gases alone (the largest: Na): transit 2.7 to 6.0 ppm rms, most of it a constant offset of 3 to 5 ppm. ([Validation: Atmosphere: transmission and emission spectra](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-atmosphere); `test/rt_reference.test.mjs`)
- The same, with the tables interpolated our way (log σ in 1/T) and not petitRADTRANS's (σ in T): up to 85 ppm in the far wings of the CO bands, 9.2 ppm rms. ([Validation: Atmosphere: transmission and emission spectra](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-atmosphere); `test/rt_reference.test.mjs`)
- The tables the app ships (R = 200, 12 g-points, 2 MB per gas), at R = 100, four molecules: 10.4 ppm rms on the low-gravity planet, 3.6 ppm on the hot Jupiter. ([Validation: Atmosphere: transmission and emission spectra](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-atmosphere); `test/rt_reference.test.mjs`)
- The shipped tables, eight molecules: 13.5 ppm rms. ([Validation: Atmosphere: transmission and emission spectra](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-atmosphere); `test/rt_reference.test.mjs`)
- Power-law haze against petitRADTRANS: transit 3.0 ppm rms. ([Validation: Atmosphere: transmission and emission spectra](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-atmosphere); `test/rt_reference.test.mjs`)
- The 3D view's layers against the limb they come from: recovered to 5.5e-7. ([Validation: Atmosphere: transmission and emission spectra](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-atmosphere); `test/atmosphere.test.mjs`)
- Equilibrium chemistry table against FastChem between its nodes: 0.02 dex rms away from C/O = 1 and up to 100 × solar; 0.06 dex over the whole grid. ([Validation: Atmosphere: transmission and emission spectra](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-atmosphere); `test/chemistry.test.mjs`)
- FastChem against our own solver for the H-He-C-N-O gas: CO, CO2, H2 identical; H2O and CH4 0.01 dex rms. ([Validation: Atmosphere: transmission and emission spectra](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-atmosphere); `test/chemistry.test.mjs`)
- Energy-limited mass loss against the owner's published table (GJ 1214 b, HD 97658 b): within 0.3%. ([Validation: Atmosphere: transmission and emission spectra](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-atmosphere); `test/escape.test.mjs`)
- Escape integrated through time, closed form: rate × time and the Rayleigh enrichment recovered. ([Validation: Atmosphere: transmission and emission spectra](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-atmosphere); `test/escape.test.mjs`)
- `node test/atmosphere.test.mjs` (33 checks), `test/opacity.test.mjs` (21), `test/rt_reference.test.mjs` (63, against petitRADTRANS 3.4.0), `test/chemistry.test.mjs` (4, against FastChem 4.0.4 and our own solver), `test/escape.test.mjs` (11), `test/climate.test.mjs` (8), `test/condensation.test.mjs` (6), `test/haze.test.mjs` (8, with scipy's Bessel functions, the HITRAN files, and Huygens and Cassini measurements of Titan), `test/stellarspec.test.mjs` (6), `test/sed.test.mjs` (11, against the dust_extinction package, interferometric diameters and AstroARIADNE's published fits), `test/bundle.test.mjs` (3), `test/retrieval.test.mjs` (retrievals and Ariel's noise against ArielRad's published values). The notes behind every number, and what the comparison with petitRADTRANS taught about mixing species and interpolating tables, are in docs/guide/validation.md, "Atmosphere".

### Assumptions and limits

- One column at a time: the day-night option interpolates between two given profiles; there are no winds, no hot-spot offset, no difference between the two limbs.
- Chemistry is gas phase and in equilibrium (with at most a quench level); condensation is applied to its result afterwards. There is no photochemistry, so no hazes are produced by the model; hazes and clouds are put in by hand.
- The self-consistent profile has a grey solution's shape. It meets the planet's total energy budget but not each layer's; real upper atmospheres are cooler than a grey closure gives. Inversions form where the gas absorbs starlight better than it holds heat, and settle; whether a given planet has one is for its data to say. No radiative-convective profile from another code was compared.
- Condensation removes gases by published vapour-pressure and condensation curves and rains them out; the chemistry is not solved again without the condensed elements, nothing lifts material back up, and a cloud's thickness and grain size are still set by hand. The Titan haze is spheres of tholin with an effective size tuned to Cassini's occultations, not fractal aggregates.
- The energy-limited rate can be wrong by a factor of several either way and ignores recombination-limited and core-powered loss; the planet's radius, mass and orbit are held fixed over the star's history; stars other than solar analogues follow a different XUV history. No number here was compared with a measured escape rate.
- Fractionation assumes an atomic-hydrogen wind, a constant temperature, and diffusion coefficients measured for three pairs only. The crossover masses in the owner's earlier notes are not reproduced: their diffusion coefficient mixed units.
- Ionization: hydrogen, sodium and potassium only, potassium with estimated rates. The stellar ultraviolet is a blackbody for the alkalis (real stars differ by factors of several on both sides of 150 nm) and a solar-analogue history for hydrogen; no measured stellar spectrum is used; nothing photodissociates.
- Emission has no scattering and no reflected light; the star is a blackbody; the 3D view is single scattering without refraction.
- No line-by-line reference was run; the comparison with petitRADTRANS shares its opacity tables.

References: [Guillot 2010](#ref-guillot2010); [Madhusudhan & Seager 2009](#ref-madhusudhan2009); [Chubb et al. 2021](#ref-chubb2021); [Karman et al. 2019](#ref-karman2019); [Mollière et al. 2019](#ref-molliere2019); [Heng & Kitzmann 2017](#ref-heng2017); [Stock et al. 2018](#ref-stock2018); [Khare et al. 1984](#ref-khare1984); [Morley et al. 2012](#ref-morley2012); [Visscher et al. 2010](#ref-visscher2010); [Wakeford et al. 2017](#ref-wakeford2017); [Robinson et al. 2014](#ref-robinson2014); [Mikal-Evans et al. 2019](#ref-mikalevans2019); [Lodders 2003](#ref-lodders2003); [Fray & Schmitt 2009](#ref-frayschmitt2009); [Atreya & Wong 2005](#ref-atreya2005); [Fulchignoni et al. 2005](#ref-fulchignoni2005); [Niemann et al. 2010](#ref-niemann2010); [Asplund et al. 2021](#ref-asplund2021); [Kitzmann & Heng 2018](#ref-kitzmann2018); [Line & Parmentier 2016](#ref-line2016); [Watson et al. 1981](#ref-watson1981); [Erkaev et al. 2007](#ref-erkaev2007); [Hunten et al. 1987](#ref-hunten1987); [Zahnle & Kasting 1986](#ref-zahnle1986); [Ribas et al. 2005](#ref-ribas2005); [Verner et al. 1996](#ref-verner1996); [Verner & Ferland 1996](#ref-vernerferland1996); [Voronov 1997](#ref-voronov1997); [Pearson 2019](#ref-pearson2019).

<a id="derived"></a>

## 19. Derived quantities and uncertainty propagation

Code: `src/core/derive.js`, `src/core/session.js (summarizeFit)`, `src/main.js`, `src/core/stellar.js`, `src/core/hz.js`

The system table (modelled on Table 7 of [Pearson et al. 2022](#ref-pearson2022)) is computed from the fitted parameters and the stellar inputs:

| Quantity | Expression |
| --- | --- |
| transit depth | $k^2$ (geometric, no limb darkening) |
| planet radius | $k\,R_\star$ |
| semi-major axis | $(a/R_\star)\,R_\star$ |
| impact parameter | $b = (a/R_\star)\cos i\,(1-e^2)/(1+e\sin\omega)$; at eclipse with $1 - e\sin\omega$ |
| durations, eclipse and periastron times | numerical, see [Kepler solver and orbits](#orbits) |
| stellar density | $\rho_\star = 3\pi (a/R_\star)^3/(G P^2)$ (planet mass neglected) |
| equilibrium temperature | $T_\mathrm{eq} = T_\mathrm{eff}\sqrt{R_\star/2a}$ (zero albedo, full redistribution, at the semi-major axis) |
| insolation | $R_\star^2\,(T_\mathrm{eff}/5772\,\mathrm{K})^4/a^2$ in Earth units, $a$ in au |
| velocity semi-amplitude | $K$ of [Radial velocities](#rv), when the planet has a mass |
| planet density | from $M_p$ and $k R_\star$ |

### Propagation

Derived quantities are computed on equal-weight posterior draws (600), one evaluation per draw, and summarised by the median and the 15.87% and 84.13% quantiles, so correlations between parameters are carried through. In the analyzer, $R_\star$, $M_\star$ and $T_\mathrm{eff}$ are drawn for each sample from normal distributions with their input uncertainties, unless they were fitted or are tied through Kepler's law or the velocities, in which case the fitted or held values are used. In the headless path (`runSession`, the Python package) the stellar values are used as given, **without** their uncertainties, unless they were free parameters.

### Stellar mass and radius

When only $T_\mathrm{eff}$, $\log g$ and [Fe/H] are known, mass and radius come from the eclipsing-binary calibration of [Torres, Andersen & Giménez 2010](#ref-torres2010), with its scatter (0.027 dex in $\log M$, 0.014 dex in $\log R$) added in quadrature to the propagated input errors; the result is flagged as extrapolated below 0.6 $M_\odot$ or outside 3800 to 10000 K.

### Habitable zone

The limits are the effective fluxes of [Kopparapu et al. 2013](#ref-kopparapu2013); [Kopparapu et al. 2014](#ref-kopparapu2014), $S_\mathrm{eff} = S_\odot + aT + bT^2 + cT^3 + dT^4$ with $T = T_\mathrm{eff} - 5780$ K (clamped to 2600 to 7200 K), converted to $d/R_\star = 215.032\,(T_\mathrm{eff}/5780)^2/\sqrt{S_\mathrm{eff}}$. The band drawn is averaged over the $T_\mathrm{eff}$ uncertainty and an albedo range; the albedo scaling is a heuristic of this application, not part of the published limits.

### Accuracy and checks

- Velocity semi-amplitude of Jupiter and Earth against astropy constants: 12.474 and 0.08947 m/s in both. ([Validation: Estimates in the catalogue](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-relations); `test/relations.test.mjs`)
- Dwarf masses against Torres et al. 2010: within 0.022 dex (that calibration’s own scatter is 0.027). ([Validation: Estimates in the catalogue](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-relations); `test/relations.test.mjs`)
- For HD 80606 b the catalogue look-up selects [Pearson et al. 2022](#ref-pearson2022) and the system table is compared with its Table 7 in `node test/catalog.test.mjs`; the eclipse duration is the exception described under [Kepler solver and orbits](#orbits).

### Assumptions and limits

- A planet radius or mass in physical units is only as good as the stellar radius and mass. If the star was held fixed, the quoted uncertainty of $R_p$, $a$ and $M_p$ excludes the stellar uncertainty in the headless path and includes it only through the resampling described above in the analyzer. State which applies.
- The equilibrium temperature assumes zero albedo and full redistribution. The transit depth is $k^2$, not the limb-darkened minimum of the light curve.
- The Torres calibration returns 1.05 $M_\odot$ and 1.02 $R_\odot$ for solar inputs, the known offset of that relation.

References: [Pearson et al. 2022](#ref-pearson2022); [Torres, Andersen & Giménez 2010](#ref-torres2010); [Kopparapu et al. 2013](#ref-kopparapu2013); [Kopparapu et al. 2014](#ref-kopparapu2014); [Winn 2010](#ref-winn2010).

<a id="catalogue"></a>

## 20. Catalogue sources, merging and provenance

Code: `src/core/catalog.js`, `src/core/sources/`, `src/core/relations.js`, `tools/build_catalog.py`, `tools/build_catalog_table.py`, `tools/build_catalog_eu.py`, `tools/build_esl_catalog.py`

### Sources

The site works from dated snapshots, because the archives cannot be queried from a browser page. (1) The NASA Exoplanet Archive [Akeson et al. 2013](#ref-akeson2013) Planetary Systems table `ps`, every published reference of every planet, and the composite table `pscomppars`, through its TAP service. (2) The Extrasolar Planets Encyclopaedia, exoplanet.eu [Schneider et al. 2011](#ref-schneider2011), from its CSV export. (3) The TESS Objects of Interest table [Guerrero et al. 2021](#ref-guerrero2021) as served by the NASA archive. Each snapshot records its date, query and row counts; the merged offline catalogue (`public/esl-catalog/`) carries checksums of its inputs.

### Choosing the parameters of a planet

For a look-up in the analyzer, every reference of the planet is scored and the highest score is used (`chooseParameters`): 100 × completeness (weighted by what the chosen kind of analysis needs; a derivable quantity counts in part) + consistency (−25 per failed check, −60 per fatal one, −8 per warning, +1.5 per passed check up to 6) + recency (up to 3) + small terms (the archive's default flag, stellar parameters from the same paper, candidates and controversial planets marked down). The consistency checks compare a reported quantity with the value implied by the reference's other numbers and count the difference in $\sigma$ with a fractional floor: $a/R_\star$ against Kepler's third law; stellar density from $a/R_\star$ and $P$ against $M_\star$, $R_\star$; $\log g$ against $M_\star$, $R_\star$; $a$ against $(a/R_\star)R_\star$; the impact parameter; the transit duration (numerical); the depth against $k^2$; $k$ against the radii; $K$ against the mass; periastron outside the star; the transit geometry. A difference up to $3\sigma$ passes, up to $5\sigma$ warns, beyond fails.

Whatever the chosen reference lacks is filled in a fixed order and **labelled**: reported by the chosen reference; derived from its own numbers; taken from another reference (named); derived from a mix; assumed (for example $e = 0$ when only an upper limit exists, or [Fe/H] = 0). The page shows every value with its label and source, and the alternatives with their scores.

### Merging catalogues

For the Search and Plan pages the two planet catalogues are matched in stages: identical normalised names; aliases; host and planet letter; then position within 1 arcminute with periods within 3%. A match from the later stages is rejected when the positions differ by more than 0.25° (unless the periods agree to 0.1%) or the periods by more than 20%. Period and epoch are always taken from the same catalogue. Values that differ by more than $3\sigma$ and by more than a per-quantity floor are marked as disagreeing. For the planner, the ephemeris is the published ($P$, $T_0$) pair that predicts the smallest timing uncertainty today, $\sqrt{\sigma_{T_0}^2 + (N\sigma_P)^2}$.

### Estimates

Missing quantities are estimated from named relations, never overwriting a catalogue value, and marked as estimates (with a flag when an estimate is built on another estimate): the mass-radius relation of [Chen & Kipping 2017](#ref-chen2017) (no mass above the radius where it stops being single-valued); the dwarf sequence of [Pecaut & Mamajek 2013](#ref-pecaut2013); [Torres, Andersen & Giménez 2010](#ref-torres2010); and exact geometry for depth [Seager & Mallén-Ornelas 2003](#ref-seager2003), duration and impact parameter [Winn 2010](#ref-winn2010), equilibrium temperature (zero albedo, full redistribution) and $K$. The relation of [Otegi, Bouchy & Helled 2020](#ref-otegi2020) is implemented as an alternative.

### Accuracy and checks

- Chen & Kipping mass-radius relation against forecaster: largest difference 1.37%. ([Validation: Estimates in the catalogue](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-relations); `test/relations.test.mjs`)
- Pecaut & Mamajek dwarf sequence against the published table: 63 rows, B9V to M9.5V, identical. ([Validation: Estimates in the catalogue](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-relations); `test/relations.test.mjs`)
- Dwarf masses against Torres et al. 2010: within 0.022 dex (that calibration’s own scatter is 0.027). ([Validation: Estimates in the catalogue](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-relations); `test/relations.test.mjs`)
- Snapshot of 2026-11-15 (the index files under `public/catalog*/` and `public/esl-catalog/manifest.json`): 40,414 rows of `ps` for 6,470 planets around 4,862 hosts; 8,479 exoplanet.eu planets; 8,175 TOIs; 8,561 planets in the merged catalogue, 6,388 matched in both (5,882 by name, 254 by alias, 31 by host and letter, 221 by position).
- Selection logic on constructed references with planted inconsistencies and on real systems: `node test/catalog.test.mjs`, `node test/sources.test.mjs`, `node test/eslcatalog.test.mjs`.

### Assumptions and limits

- The scoring weights and thresholds are judgement calls, not calibrated against anything. The chosen reference is a starting point; a paper should cite the original publications of the values it uses, which the provenance labels identify.
- Catalogue values are not re-derived from data. Time systems are flagged but not converted. Choosing an ephemeris by its quoted errors favours publications with optimistic errors.
- Population relations have large scatter and are not measurements. Estimated values must not be reported as measured.
- TOIs are not matched to confirmed planets. Only the offline path of the merged-catalogue builder has been run.

References: [Akeson et al. 2013](#ref-akeson2013); [Schneider et al. 2011](#ref-schneider2011); [Guerrero et al. 2021](#ref-guerrero2021); [Chen & Kipping 2017](#ref-chen2017); [Otegi, Bouchy & Helled 2020](#ref-otegi2020); [Pecaut & Mamajek 2013](#ref-pecaut2013); [Torres, Andersen & Giménez 2010](#ref-torres2010); [Seager & Mallén-Ornelas 2003](#ref-seager2003); [Winn 2010](#ref-winn2010).

<a id="observability"></a>

## 21. Observability and sky positions

Code: `src/core/observability.js`, `src/core/astro.js`, `src/core/asteroids.js`, `src/core/horizon.js`, `src/core/skyfield.js`, `src/core/healpix.js`

Two modules compute positions; both take UT1 = UTC and use the algorithms of [Meeus 1998](#ref-meeus1998): IAU 1976 precession, the mean sidereal time of 1982, a four-term nutation, the low-precision Sun (chapter 25) and a truncated lunar theory (chapter 47). The sky view (`astro.js`) adds the planets from the Keplerian elements of [Standish & Williams (JPL)](#ref-standish) with light-time iteration, apparent sidereal time, and refraction for display by the formulas of Bennett and Sæmundsson as given by [Meeus 1998](#ref-meeus1998) (see also [Bennett 1982](#ref-bennett1982)). The planner (`observability.js`) uses mean sidereal time for the target, topocentric parallax for the Moon, and the airmass of [Kasten & Young 1989](#ref-kasten1989).

### Which transits are observable

Transit $n$ is at $T_n = T_0 + nP$, converted from $\mathrm{BJD}_\mathrm{TDB}$ to UTC, with ingress and egress at $T_n \mp T_{14}/2$. Its mid-time uncertainty is

$$
\sigma_n = \sqrt{\sigma_{T_0}^2 + (n\,\sigma_P)^2}
$$

which assumes $T_0$ and $P$ uncorrelated. A transit is listed as observable in full when the whole region of interest, from one hour before ingress to one hour after egress, has the target above 30° altitude with the Sun below −18°; complete transits with a shorter baseline, and partial ones, are listed as such. All three limits are settings. Rise, set and twilight times are found by sampling every 10 minutes and bisecting.

### Ranking score

Events that pass the limits are ranked by a score of 0 to 100 (`scoreTransit`): 40 × the observable fraction of the event; 15 × the fraction of the wanted baseline that is dark, averaged over the two sides; 20 × an altitude term, the mean airmass $\bar X$ of the observable ingress, mid and egress scaled from the airmass at the altitude limit (0) to the zenith (1); 20 × a signal term; and 5 × a Moon term (1 when it is down or more than 40° away, otherwise reduced in proportion to its illuminated fraction and proximity). The signal term is the expected transit signal-to-noise for a small telescope,

$$
\mathrm{S/N} = \frac{\delta}{\sigma_1}\sqrt{T_{14}/1\,\mathrm{min}}, \qquad \sigma_1 = \sqrt{\left(2000\,\mathrm{ppm}\times10^{0.2(m-12)}\right)^2 + (400\,\mathrm{ppm})^2}
$$

with $\delta$ the depth and $m$ the catalogued magnitude of the host ($V$, or TESS $T$ when that is all there is): photon noise of a 0.3–0.4 m telescope per minute and a floor for scintillation and systematics. It scores 0 at S/N 5 and full marks at S/N 200 on a logarithmic scale; an event without a depth or a magnitude, and every eclipse or phase window, gets half marks. The score is a ranking aid: the noise model is not a given telescope's.

### Bright asteroids and paths

The sky view draws eight bright asteroids (Ceres, Pallas, Juno, Vesta, Hebe, Iris, Hygiea, Eunomia) from osculating elements of the JPL Small-Body Database bundled in `asteroids.js` (epoch JD 2461200.5 TDB, ecliptic J2000), propagated as two-body orbits about the Sun (Kepler's equation as for the planets), with light-time iteration and the Earth of `astro.js`; magnitudes are the IAU $H, G$ system of Bowell et al. (1989) with $H$ and $G$ from the same database. A card's "Show path" draws where a satellite (SGP4), the Moon, a planet or an asteroid goes: across the sky tonight, or among the stars over ±3 days to ±6 months (drawn in J2000, so it turns with the stars), with time or date ticks.

Against JPL Horizons (geocentric astrometric RA and Dec, five dates from 200 days before the epoch to a year after, `test/asteroids.test.mjs`): at most 56″ within 200 days of the epoch and 138″ a year after it (Hygiea; the other seven under 40″), magnitudes within 0.003 mag. Perturbations by the planets are not modelled, so the error keeps growing away from the epoch; the elements are refreshed by `test/make_asteroid_reference.py`.

### Terrain horizon

The horizon profile is traced through elevation tiles (Mapzen/Tilezen Terrarium) along great circles out to 150 km on a spherical Earth, with terrestrial refraction through an effective radius $R/(1 - k)$, $k$ = 0.13.

### Survey image of a field

The sky view shows a real image of a target's field from an open survey (DSS2, 2MASS, Pan-STARRS DR1, SDSS DR9, DESI Legacy Surveys DR10 or AllWISE, as HiPS maps of CDS). Each image is a square of 512 pixels on one gnomonic (TAN) plane about the target [Calabretta & Greisen 2002](#ref-calabretta2002), north up and east to the left; neighbouring images lie on the same plane, so the mosaic and its overlays stay continuous. The page resamples the survey's HiPS tiles onto that grid itself (nearest pixel, at the shallowest tile order whose pixels are no larger than the image's): each output pixel's direction is located in the HEALPix nested scheme of Górski et al. (2005) at the order of the tile pixels, its upper bits naming the tile and its lower bits the pixel inside it. CDS hips2fits, given the same WCS, is the fallback.

The stars are Gaia DR3 [Gaia Collaboration, Vallenari et al. 2023](#ref-gaia2023) from VizieR [Ochsenbein, Bauer & Marcout 2000](#ref-ochsenbein2000), moved to the date shown by their proper motions. The target is the Gaia star nearest to the catalogue position within 8″, the one closest to the catalogue's V when several are; a neighbour is a possible comparison star when its $\Delta G = G - G_\star$ lies in the chosen range, Gaia does not flag it as variable, it is more than 10″ from the target and, with a detector outline, inside the outline. Separations are the haversine formula; position angles, east of north, are

$$
\theta = \mathrm{atan2}\left(\sin\Delta\alpha\cos\delta_2,\ \cos\delta_1\sin\delta_2 - \sin\delta_1\cos\delta_2\cos\Delta\alpha\right)
$$

### Accuracy and checks

- Stars, altitude and azimuth: max 25.2″ (20″ of it is annual aberration, not modelled). ([Validation: Positions in the sky](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-sky); `test/astro.test.mjs`)
- Sun: max 33.8″. ([Validation: Positions in the sky](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-sky); `test/astro.test.mjs`)
- Moon: max 12.2″. ([Validation: Positions in the sky](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-sky); `test/astro.test.mjs`)
- Saturn (the worst planet): max 10.0′. ([Validation: Positions in the sky](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-sky); `test/astro.test.mjs`)
- Sidereal time: max 0.30″. ([Validation: Positions in the sky](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-sky); `test/astro.test.mjs`)
- Refraction above 10°: max 6.30″. ([Validation: Positions in the sky](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-sky); `test/astro.test.mjs`)
- Target altitude, 400 positions: worst 0.0077°. ([Validation: Which transits can be observed](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-planner); `test/observability.test.mjs`)
- Sunset, sunrise and the three twilights, 274 crossings: worst 6.4 s. ([Validation: Which transits can be observed](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-planner); `test/observability.test.mjs`)
- Barycentric time correction (BJD_TDB − JD_UTC): worst 3.92 s. ([Validation: Which transits can be observed](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-planner); `test/observability.test.mjs`)
- Swarthmore finder: mid-transit times: 32 events, worst 0.70 min. ([Validation: Which transits can be observed](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-planner); `test/observability.test.mjs`)
- Swarthmore finder: elevations: worst 0.52°. ([Validation: Which transits can be observed](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-planner); `test/observability.test.mjs`)

### Assumptions and limits

- Positions are good enough to find and frame a target and to decide observability, not for astrometry: annual aberration of stars (20″), proper motion, parallax and polar motion are not modelled, and Jupiter and Saturn are limited to about 10′ by the simple elements.
- Planner altitudes are geometric (no refraction). The planner's barycentric correction uses the Sun's centre and is good to about 4 s.
- The ephemeris uncertainty ignores the covariance of $T_0$ and $P$ and trusts the published errors; an ephemeris that is stale or optimistic gives a window that is too narrow.
- The comparison with the Swarthmore transit finder covers one site and one week. Terrain data have 30 m to 300 m pixels and contain no buildings or trees; summits come out 0.08° to 0.14° low in the three places checked.
- Survey images are for finding a field and judging its comparison stars, not for photometry: they are the survey's display images (JPEG or PNG, stretched), resampled to the nearest pixel. ΔG is in Gaia's G band, not the observer's filter. The hips2fits fallback has not been seen to answer (CDS returned HTTP 404 on 2026-11-16), so its use of the WCS is untested.

References: [Meeus 1998](#ref-meeus1998); [Standish & Williams (JPL)](#ref-standish); [Bennett 1982](#ref-bennett1982); [Kasten & Young 1989](#ref-kasten1989); [Jensen 2013](#ref-jensen2013); [Astropy Collaboration 2022](#ref-astropy2022); [Anderson & Francis 2012](#ref-anderson2012); [Calabretta & Greisen 2002](#ref-calabretta2002); [Gaia Collaboration, Vallenari et al. 2023](#ref-gaia2023); [Ochsenbein, Bauer & Marcout 2000](#ref-ochsenbein2000).

<a id="photometry"></a>

## 22. Image photometry

Code: `src/core/photometry.js`, `src/core/fits.js`, `src/photometry/pipeline.js`, `src/photometry/transitfit.js`

The photometry page turns a stack of FITS frames, or a TESS, Kepler or K2 target pixel file, into a differential light curve. The method follows EXOTIC [Zellem et al. 2020](#ref-zellem2020), with the differences listed below. Pixel centres are at integer coordinates.

- **Sky.** The median of the pixels whose centres lie in an annulus around the star, after iterative clipping at 3σ about the median (5 iterations). The annulus starts 2 px outside the aperture.
- **Centroid.** A flux-weighted centroid above a threshold of 3σ over the local sky in a box, re-centred until it moves by less than 0.01 px, followed by a Gaussian-windowed centroid. Stars are tracked from frame to frame; when the field jumps, rotates or flips (meridian flip), sources are re-detected and matched by triangle similarity [Groth 1986](#ref-groth1986); [Valdes et al. 1995](#ref-valdes1995); [Beroiz et al. 2020](#ref-beroiz2020) and a similarity transform is fitted.
- **Aperture sum.** The exact overlap area of a circle (or an ellipse of the same area) with each pixel, the algorithm of photutils [Bradley et al. (Photutils)](#ref-bradley). Flux = sum − area × sky.
- **PSF photometry.** An elliptical Gaussian, $B + A\exp[-(x'^2/2\sigma_x^2 + y'^2/2\sigma_y^2)]$ with flux $2\pi A\sigma_x\sigma_y$, or a Moffat profile, $B + A(1 + r^2/\gamma^2)^{-\beta}$ with flux $\pi A\gamma^2/(\beta - 1)$, fitted to a box by unweighted Levenberg-Marquardt with analytic derivatives; the model is averaged over each pixel when the star is undersampled.
- **Optimal extraction.** The sky-limited estimator of [Naylor 1998](#ref-naylor1998) with a Gaussian profile $P$ taken from the brightest well-fitted star of the frame: $F = \sum P\,(d - B)/\sum P^2$. The pixel variance is assumed uniform.
- **Comparison stars.** The target's flux is divided by one comparison star or by the unweighted sum of all of them; the alternative "no comparison star" is always tried.
- **Choice of aperture, annulus and comparison.** Every combination of 12 aperture radii from 1.5 to 6 times the PSF σ of the first frame, 4 annulus widths from 6 to 15σ, each comparison choice, and the PSF and optimal fluxes, is reduced to a light curve; the one with the smallest scatter of residuals is kept. The residuals are from a least-squares fit of the transit model of this document, through the same likelihood, with EXOTIC's bounds (Rp/R★ up to 1.25 times the catalogue value, the mid-transit time within 25σ, the inclination within 5°), times the chosen detrending: airmass, $a_1 e^{a_2 X}$ (EXOTIC's), or a linear or quadratic polynomial in time fitted with the transit (a night without an airmass falls back to a line in time). The planet's parameters are typed or taken from the site's catalogue by the target's name; without them the candidates are ranked by a quick least-squares fit of a trapezoidal transit and a baseline instead, and the report says so.
- **Calibration.** Bias, dark and flat frames found among the files (IMAGETYP, OBSTYPE or the file name) are combined pixel by pixel with the median. The master dark and master flat have the master bias subtracted; the flat is divided by its median. Each light frame becomes (frame − bias − dark) / flat; pixels where the flat is below 0.05 are blanked.
- **Airmass** is read from the header or computed as $\sec z$.
- **Time.** Mid-exposure UTC converted to $\mathrm{BJD}_\mathrm{TDB}$ as described under [Time standards](#conventions). Where the header time sits in the exposure is a setting: the start (half the exposure time, from EXPTIME or its equivalents, is added; the FITS meaning of DATE-OBS), the middle (used as it is), or as the time keyword's comment says (half the exposure added only when it says "start", EXOTIC's convention). A keyword that is a mid-exposure time by name (JD-MID, DATE-AVG) is never shifted.
- **Limb darkening.** The four Claret coefficients of the transit model are typed, or computed from the star's $T_\mathrm{eff}$, $\log g$ and [Fe/H] (from the site's catalogue or typed) for the chosen filter: trilinear interpolation in the bundled PHOENIX table [Husser et al. 2013](#ref-husser2013) that the analyzer uses, or the grey-atmosphere estimate of [Transit model and limb darkening](#transit) when the filter is not in the table.

### Uncertainties

The uncertainty attached to every point of the exported light curve is one number: the robust scatter (1.4826 × median absolute deviation) of the residuals of the fit just described, relative to the median flux. A photon-noise estimate is computed for diagnosis only,

$$
\sigma_F^2 = \frac{F}{g} + n_\mathrm{pix}\,\sigma_\mathrm{sky}^2\left(1 + \frac{n_\mathrm{pix}}{n_\mathrm{sky}}\right), \qquad \frac{\sigma_R}{R} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_T^2}{T^2} + \frac{\sigma_C^2}{C^2}}
$$

in ADU, with $g$ the gain in e⁻/ADU (from the header keywords GAIN or EGAIN, or typed; when it is unknown the photon term is left out and the estimate is the sky-limited one, said as such), $\sigma_\mathrm{sky}$ the scatter in the annulus (which contains sky, read and dark noise), $n_\mathrm{pix}$ the aperture area, $n_\mathrm{sky}$ the annulus area, and $R = T/C$ the ratio of target to comparison.

### Detrending

For pointing-driven systematics (K2, TESS) two detrenders are offered: the self-flat-field of [Vanderburg & Johnson 2014](#ref-vanderburg2014) (flux against arclength along the principal axis of the centroids, in windows, with a running-median trend removed) and a Gaussian process with a squared-exponential kernel on the centroid coordinates (optionally time), whose hyperparameters maximise the marginal likelihood on a subset of points; the light curve is divided by 1 + trend.

### Accuracy and checks

- Aperture sums with exact pixel overlap, 4 radii × 6 stars: 4.4e-16 relative. ([Validation: From images to a light curve](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-photometry); `test/photometry.test.mjs`)
- Flux-weighted centroid: 1.4e-14 px. ([Validation: From images to a light curve](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-photometry); `test/photometry.test.mjs`)
- Star detection: the same six stars as DAOStarFinder, within 0.03 px. ([Validation: From images to a light curve](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-photometry); `test/photometry.test.mjs`)
- FITS pixel values, six data types: 3.7e-16. ([Validation: From images to a light curve](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-photometry); `test/fits.test.mjs`)
- End to end on synthetic frames with an injected transit: scatter 0.372%, at the photon-noise level. ([Validation: From images to a light curve](https://exoplanet.science/methods/#val-photometry); `test/photometry.test.mjs`)
- EXOTIC's sample frames (HAT-P-32 b, 142 MicroObservatory frames) reduced by both codes: `node test/exotic_photometry.test.mjs`. The numbers are in the reproducibility table below; the two reductions choose different apertures and comparison stars and their $R_p/R_\star$ differ by 2.3σ.

### Assumptions and limits

- The exported error bars are a single empirical scatter, the same for every point; they do not follow airmass, clouds or the star's count rate, and they include any real signal that the trapezoid does not describe. There is no read-noise or scintillation term in the per-point estimate. Without a gain the photon noise of the stars is not counted anywhere (no 1 e⁻/ADU is assumed): the signal-to-noise figures of the inspection tools then use the measured sky noise alone and say so.
- Choosing the aperture and comparison star that minimise the residual scatter of a transit fit is a selection on the data: it can bias the scatter low. On EXOTIC's sample the choice of comparison star moves $R_p/R_\star$ by more than its formal uncertainty.
- Darks are not scaled by exposure time: dark frames must have the light frames' exposure (or be left out). The flat is not dark-subtracted. There is no saturation or non-linearity correction beyond flagging saturated stars and leaving them out of the comparison candidates.
- Checked on synthetic frames, two archived TESS and Kepler pixel files, and one set of real ground-based frames compared with EXOTIC's reduction of the same frames; no reduction here has been compared with a published light curve. At EXOTIC's own aperture this code's scatter is higher (0.599% against 0.573%) and the reason was not found.
- HCOMPRESS-compressed FITS files are not read.

References: [Zellem et al. 2020](#ref-zellem2020); [Bradley et al. (Photutils)](#ref-bradley); [Naylor 1998](#ref-naylor1998); [Groth 1986](#ref-groth1986); [Valdes et al. 1995](#ref-valdes1995); [Beroiz et al. 2020](#ref-beroiz2020); [Vanderburg & Johnson 2014](#ref-vanderburg2014); [Merline & Howell 1995](#ref-merline1995); [Ricker et al. 2014](#ref-ricker2015); [Borucki et al. 2010](#ref-borucki2010).

<a id="spacelc"></a>

## 23. TESS, Kepler and K2 light curves: quality, stitching, transit-aware detrending, K2 systematics

Code: `src/core/lcprep.js`, `src/core/k2.js`, `src/core/zip.js`, `src/photometry/prep.js`, `src/photometry/mast.js`

The photometry page lists every product the public MAST bucket holds for a star (SPOC 2-minute and 20-second postage stamps, TESS-SPOC and QLP products of the full-frame images, Kepler and K2 long and short cadence; light curves and target pixel files) and loads one product per sector, as the owner's TOI extraction does: 20 s and 2 min of the same sector are the same photons and must not both enter a likelihood. A target pixel file is reduced with the aperture search of the previous section.

- **Quality.** lightkurve's bitmasks [Lightkurve Collaboration 2018](#ref-lightkurve2018): 'default' (TESS 17087, Kepler and K2 1130799) unless another preset is chosen. Light-curve files: PDCSAP (or SAP) with the same mask.
- **Stitching.** Each sector (quarter, campaign) is divided by its own median; a cadence less than 1 s after another is dropped.
- **Transit mask.** Points with $|((t - T_0 + P/2) \;\mathrm{mod}\;P) - P/2| < 1.5\,T_{14}/2$ for any known planet, $T_{14} = (P/\pi)\,\mathrm{arcsin}\left(\sqrt{(1+k)^2 - b^2}/(a/R_\star \sin i)\right)$ (with the eccentric factor); planets from the catalogue and the TOI list [Guerrero et al. 2021](#ref-guerrero2021), or typed.
- **Trend.** wotan's time-windowed biweight [Hippke et al. 2019](#ref-hippke2019): for every point, Tukey's biweight location (c = 5, from the median and the MAD, iterated to $10^{-6}$ MAD) of the unmasked points within $\pm w/2$, segments split at gaps longer than 1 h. With "auto" the window $w$ is chosen per sector by injecting box transits of the longest duration (1500 ppm) away from the real ones, unmasked, and maximising recovered depth × $\sqrt{T_{14}/\Delta t}$ / noise (EXOTIC's optimize_window).
- **Clip and trim.** 4σ about a Savitzky–Golay smooth of 30 min, never in transit; 30 min after every gap longer than an hour.
- **Windows.** $\pm 2.5\,T_{14}$ around every predicted transit with points inside it; another planet's transit in a window is reported and, when its geometry is known, divided out.
- **K2.** Pixel-level decorrelation [Deming et al. 2015](#ref-deming2015) as EVEREST [Luger et al. 2016](#ref-luger2016); [Luger et al. 2018](#ref-luger2018) and lightkurve's PLDCorrector set it up for K2: the 3σ threshold-mask pixels over the aperture flux, their products to third order (16 principal components per order), the principal components of the background pixels (below the median image, normalised), a degree-5 B-spline in time with $n/50$ columns for the star, fitted jointly by least squares with Gaussian priors (10× the flux scatter) and 5σ clipping, five times; the pixel and background parts are removed. Thruster firings are flagged from QUALITY bits 20 and 21 and from 5σ jumps of the centroid along the roll arc [Vanderburg & Johnson 2014](#ref-vanderburg2014).
- **CDPP** is lightkurve's estimate_cdpp (Savitzky–Golay flatten, 5σ clip, the standard deviation of a 13-cadence running mean), with both lengths scaled from Kepler's 29.4-minute cadence when sectors of other cadences are compared.
- **Zips.** Zip archives are read from their central directory (ZIP64 included); a deflated entry becomes the slice of the archive between a 10-byte gzip header and a trailer made from the directory's CRC-32 and size, so frames are inflated one at a time as the pipeline reads them.

### Accuracy and checks

- Against lightkurve 2.6 on the WASP-18 (TESS), TrES-2 (Kepler) and K2-3 (K2) pixel files: the cadences of every quality preset, times to 0 µs, aperture flux 3e-7 and centroids 3e-7 of the CCD coordinate (lightkurve sums float32), SAP_FLUX of the pipeline's light-curve files to 1.2e-7, threshold masks identical, CDPP to 4e-5: `node test/tpf_lightkurve.test.mjs`.
- Biweight trend against wotan to 1.9e-9 with and without transit masks, EXOTIC's T14, mask, clip, trim, binning, window injection (7e-7) and alias scan exactly, lightkurve's flatten (5e-12) and CDPP (1e-8), the chain on TrES-2's pixels (trend 2.4e-7, depth 13184 ppm both): `node test/lcprep.test.mjs`.
- K2-3, campaign 1, CDPP at 6.5 h: raw SAP 5822 ppm; self-flat-field 326 ppm (lightkurve SFFCorrector 158); PLD order 3 40.2 ppm (lightkurve PLDCorrector 48.0; the pipeline's PDCSAP 186); thruster firings from the centroid match 154 of 172 flagged cadences: `node test/k2.test.mjs`.
- Zips written by Python's zipfile (stored, deflated, ZIP64, nested, .fits.gz inside) and EXOTIC's sample-data zip: `node test/zip.test.mjs`.

### Assumptions and limits

- TESScut cutouts, TGLC, K2SFF and EVEREST light curves cannot be fetched from a page (no CORS, or not in the bucket). Sectors of different cadence go to the analyzer as one light curve with one exposure time (the median); the analyzer does not yet read the window index the hand-off carries ("Split by orbit" does the same).
- The self-flat-field here is worse than lightkurve's on the whole K2-3 campaign (326 against 158 ppm) and better on its first 24 days; the reason was not found. Dropping the unflagged thruster firings did not lower the CDPP of K2-3.
- The window injection is EXOTIC's procedure; its point counts are scaled for cadences coarser than 2 min, and on a quiet star (TrES-2) every window recovers the injected depth equally, so the choice is then arbitrary.

References: [Hippke et al. 2019](#ref-hippke2019); [Lightkurve Collaboration 2018](#ref-lightkurve2018); [Guerrero et al. 2021](#ref-guerrero2021); [Deming et al. 2015](#ref-deming2015); [Luger et al. 2016](#ref-luger2016); [Luger et al. 2018](#ref-luger2018); [Vanderburg & Johnson 2014](#ref-vanderburg2014).

<a id="imexam"></a>

## 24. Image inspection, focus and comparison stars
